A GRIEVANCE ! At the burial of a poor man in the Danish churchyard at Frederiksted about a fortnight ago an occurrence took place, which filled the minds of those attending the funeral with the utmost indignation. The fact is that from want of the rope, by which the coffin was to be lowered down, it was handed down to two men standing in the grave, and these not being strong enough, the coffin was tilted, so the lid was knocked off, and the corpse not only became visible, but was even half thrown out of the coffin. And this was not the only disgraceful thing on this occasion. At the ceremony of casting earth upon the coffin the parson had to wield one of the large, clumsy hoes that had been used in digging the grave, because the little handspade else used on such occasions was not there either. We are not aware, whether the apparatus requisite at burials be the private property of the gravedigger here alluded to ; but we are perfectly convinced, that that privilege, which he is exercising so freely, of levying exorbitant taxes at the funerals of the more wealthy, of necessity implies, that, in case a burial free of expense has been grunted to h poor person, it is also then his duty to furnish the implements indispensably necessary at a decent performance of this serious ceremony; for every right has its corresponding duty, and, þÿ even in the most licentious and disorderly state of things, þÿ it would be too inconsistent, that the poverty of a dead man should justify a privileged and

salaried gravedigger in refusing to assist in the ordinary manner at his interment, and thereby perhaps preventing it altogether. We take it for granted, that this scandalous scene, which we have " even the evil one can quote scripture, different mentioned is with grievance from heard quarters, entirely attributable to the gravedigger's avarice and unpardonable conduct, and as he has not with us that magic charm, which he seems to have with our Danish ministers out here, we have not hesitated in thus publicly expressing the animadversion of an indignant Public. Frederiksted, October 28th 1852. T. H. E.

IMKHFEDnC OF THE COLONIAL COUNCIL. Report to Ilia llajcsly the King from the Colonial Council for the Danish Westindia Possessions, on the draft of a law produced by the Government, regarding the Compensation to be given to the former owners of slaves. This report is essentially in conformity with that forwarded to the Council by the Committee, consisting of Messrs. 5. Wright, E. lleilhuth, II. II. Berg, II. Hanschell , F. 11. Newton. The draft of a law regarding compensation to the former owners of the unfrce in the Danish Possessions in the Westindies, has ever since it was promulgated in these colonies been the subject of so serious and universal consideration as could only be caused and maintained by the great importance of the case. This consideration has led to the common, wc might almost say unanimous opinion that the proposed indemnity ot $-10 for each unfree is so unproportionate, so little equivalent with the value of the object, this that cannot be considered as a compensation, word it meaning, as it does, a sufficient amends or a payment in full of the value. The Colonial Council cannot otherwise than fully adopt this view of the matter. The preamble of the draft laid before us contains a' reasoning through which the above amount of $40 is arrived at, and wbieli wc shall now take the liberty of examining, and shall add such remarks and elucidations as may be requisite The chief point which Government aims at establishing is, that it cannot acknowledge any legal claim on the side of the slave owners, accordingly
that no legal obligation exists for granting compensation in consequence of emancipation ; but

that the demand can only be acknowledged as a claim of justice and equity. As far as there may exist any difference beequity on the to other, tween legal right on the one side, and justice and Government do away with the same. But we deem it the duty of . without acknowledging this difference, which Government in our opinion ought not to urge, we do believe that the former slave owners possess a perfect legal claim that The assertion for compensation. the claim for compensation is not a legal one, rests on grounds which are sought for, partly in the nature which itself, partly in those occurrences of the property were connected with emancipation. Thus it is alleged that the right of the slave owners to the unfree cannot be regarded, and by the Danish Government has never been regarded, in the same light as the rights of property in objects inanimate or irrational. Moreover it is said that in juxta position to the owner's right, stands the right of the slave as a rational being ; also that slavery, in itself, is an institution contrary to religion and justice, which in civilized and as christian communities ought only to be retained long as the general welfare forbids its being abolished, but which the State is authorized and in duty bound to abolish as soon as circumstances permit. And that in such a case, as it is finally asserted, the right of property which thereby ceases to exist, cannot from its nature found any similar claim for indemnification as in those cases where the State

deprives a subject of his property for the purpose of applying it to a public purpose. But that said ease may rather be compared with an accidental misfortune falling on an individual for the sake of the community at large. We shall not here enter into any investigation whether, or how far slavery is au institution at variance with religion and justice; this being a subject about which so much has already been said, and whereon opinions arc much divided. But most assuredly, in as far as there is any fault connected with it, it was Government who in different ways encouraged the citizens and subjects to acquire such property þÿ who also founded establishments in Africa to advance the slave trade, and carried on this trade on its own account. This maybe seen for instance in the Ordinance of 12th May 1777, which reserves this traffic for the Monarch himself or his European subjects. We shall not make this case more voluminous than necessary by enumerating all these unmistakeable facts on which the right of property in slaves has been incontestibly demonstrated. They have been stated so frequently and are so generally acknowledged, that they cannot be questioned. Slaves were property both de facto and de jure, and formed not only the most intrinsic part of property in the colonies, but likewise an essential condition on which depended the preservation of other property. Nor is this right of property contested, but it as is the had not the same extent only asserted, that it right of property

in things inanimate or irrational. But because a master's right over his slaves was not unlimited, does it follow in consequence that the property can be taken away without compensation, or not tum ? Was for a nominal compensation ad libi- the master fully owner of that, the usus fructus of which was in no wise precluded by the prescribed limits, and which also according to his pleasure he could transfer to another for payment ? Property does not cease to be property because the use thereof is limited by law. This limitation, as stated in a memorial of some of the inhabitants of St. Croix to the Diet, concerns only the use of the property. " The restriction affects merely the exercise of the right, not its reality." The restriction, therefore, only has the power to regulate the use of the right as long as this right exists. A greater or a smaller, a more or a less comprehensive limitation of the right of property cannot influence the amount of compensation to be given. The limitation ceases to exist with the right of property itself. As long as it did exist it was one of the co-operative circumstances to determine the value of the property in commerce. The cessation of the right annihilates the value determined by the restriction, nor can the latter after having accomplished its effect and ceased to exist, be called upon a second time to determine the equivalent. Thus the owner of a wood is no less the owner, because the law prevents his levelling it to the ground, or his using it in a way considered

as pernicious to the public. No one would say that in consequence of these restrictions the owners could bo deprived of their property. And in the like manner it must be considered, that the slave owner cannot be despoiled of his slaves, because the law had prescribed such limits to his authority, as were called for by considerations of humanity to protect slaves from tyrannical treatment .

© m <© x ss: A T a The slave-ordinance issued by King Frederik the 5th, and quoted by the Government, in prescribing certain rules in that respect, the same time in plain words " that the slave shall has stated at be looked upon as part and share of property." The introduction to the ordinance of 16th March 1792 also points out, as not to be left out of sight, "the principle, that whereas the negroes are esteemed legal property, anything must be avoided, which has even the semblance of interference with the right of property." The limits prescribed by the law, did not preclude the owner from a judicious use of his property. The slave was bequeathed and possessed in the same manner as any other sort of property, and to the possession of a slave a pecuniary value was attached, for which he passed from the hands of one owner to those of another. This pecuniary value the owner must not be deprived of, when the State, that established and chiefly participated slaveiy, in arrives at the conviction, that the institution, acknowledged, must no longer be suffered to continue. " Let him who will gain the honor of advocating emancipation, submit to the lull burthen of what is thereby required," these words were spoken in the Diet at Boeskilde in the year 1S46, and it was there looked upon as a matter of course, that it was incumbent on the State to make the sacrifice ; an opinion also universally acknowledged throughout the world. " Your Royal Majesty's supreme justice will never permit such a violation of rights as

emancipation without compensation would be. Such a thing as this has nrt either hitherto been questioned in any other part of the world," was said in the Swedish discussions. From such principles the French terrorism only, in the year 17'j3, made a deviation, annulled however by the Consulate ten years after. We agree with Government, that the state of slavery in a civilised and christian community, ought only to be upheld as long as regard to common weal forbids to do away with it. But as it cannot be denied that the Colonies were a part of the whole, and that the inhabitants of the Colonies, who through confidence in the laws and in Government established themselves in the Danish Colonies, and there acquired this kind of property, have by emancipation lost, what the State bad ensured to them, and have thereby suffered a smaller or greater, and in many cases an entirely ruinous loss of property : thus in consequence it can neither be denied, that the welfare of such persons prohibited the annulling of slavery, unless at the same time the State would give full compensation. We also agree that a Government is not only entitled, but even in duty bound to do away with slavery as soon as circumstances admit thereof. But we can in no manner grant, that there was an' circumstance which could warrant the State to abolish slavery without full compensation. Nor can those movements which took place on the 2nd and 3rd July 1848, and of which the Governor General availed himself to decree emancipation,

be brought forward as circumstances which might justify the State in abolishing slavery without compensation ; the less so as the King's letter patent of 22nd September 1848 plainly proclaims, that Government, in granting its approbation to the act of emancipation, founded its approbation on the " vivid desire" of the negroes, and it needs no proof that vivid desires cannot justify an emancipation at the expense of the owner. This desire for liberty ought to have been considered by Government at the time when first it acknowledged slavery ; for the desire of freedom is a feeling natural with man, and must have existed even from the commencement of slavery ; but now, after having for more than a century not only acknowledged slavery as a legal institution, but even encouraged the same most strenuously, and having itself in a most extensive manner participated thereof, for Government to abolish it at the expense of the unfortunate owner, and that because the slave had a vivid desire to be free, a desire which, if not always expressed, must however always have slumbered in his soul, would not surely admit of any defence. In this case no accidental misfortune has fallen on the individual for the sake of the whole ; and this so much less, as in the following we shall have occasion to show, though it is universally acknowledged, that the emancipation is Government's own doing even from the commencement to the end. We cannot understand why the slaweowner, as maintained by Government, should not have the

same 'claim of compensation as in those cases where the State deprives any one of his property to apply it to a public aim for the sake of the whole. We admit that Government has from time to time by humane regulations tried to ameliorate the

condition of the slaves, it was nothing less than could be expected from a Christian Government, but that does not at the same time prevent Government from being just ; for the peculiar right of the owners might have continued with an amelioration of slavery, and with guarantees against arbitrary treatment of the slaves. But in the pursu- ance of such ameliorations to take away substance of property without compensation, is not alone inequitable but unjust, and even unheard of in civilised countries, where legal Government exist. This also Government has been aware of, and as soon therefore as quietude was restored after the revolt in the Duchies and the war with the Germans, steps were taken, tending to procure compensation to the negro owners ; to the amoqnt of which compensation, proposed by Government, we cannot, as mentioned beforehand, in any wise agree, as it is only a part, not a third, scarcely a fourth part of the current value ; on which we will comment in the following, but cannot refrain from observing here, that the owner has a right to full payment, and that what he gets in lieu of the property taken away from him, if Government only allows him a part, instead of what ho is entitled to, cannot be called compensation. The injustice, though less in quantity, is in principle as great as if the State refused to grant any compensation at all. Government proceeds to say : " that the same consideration þÿ (the connection of the sentence refers to measures taken for the preservation and

increase of the negroes in the colonies without importing slaves) þÿ is manifested in later and more energetic steps of Government for ameliorating the condition of the slaves, especially from the year 1834, when emancipation took place in the English Islands. Government then clearly saw, that slavery could not be continued in the Danish possessions." Here we have arrived at a point where, according to our incontrovertible opinion, the Colonies have great reason to complain ol the proceedings of Government. Whilst Government up to the issuing of the Rescript of 28th July 1847, by which the control of the owners over their T ufrec should cease after 12 years from that date, had expressed no intention of abolishing slavery, had on the contrary in several ways referred to its continuation, for instance when the representative of Government in the Colonies, in a circular of 29th July 1840 even declared, that the sugar cultivation was unconditionally dependent thereon, the abolition of slavery was notwithstanding already then meditated by Government The planters in St. Croix were prevailed on to make concessions, for example, of the free Saturday ; and front this concession, made with a view to preserve the then status quo, an argument is brought forward to prove, that Government was entitled to take all the other working days or to annull the right of property as now is done. On this and other inadmissible grounds it is further argued, that the slave owner must have been

aware, that the slave system could not last- of 1st May 1840 desired, the Governor King Christian the Eighth in a rescript in- General, to duce the planters to grant their negroes half of the Saturday. The Governor General however found, that this concession was not sufficient, and requested the alarmed planters to grant the whole day. And they complied, hoping that this would be considered satisfactory and that things would be allowed to remain in statu quo. Whatever proof therefore is founded on this and other concessions, in order to shew, that the planters must have been prepared for the entire loss of their sftves, is of no value. The reverse is the case, and such concessions could only be considered as steps taken in order to avoid further or greater losses. That no real doubts existed as to the duration of the existing system, or as to Government's will and power to uphold it, is proved by the price at which estates at that time were sold. To be continued.

DRAFT ofan Ordinance to regulate trade and profession in the Danish Westindia Possessions. Continued from our last. G Masters of vessels and of boats shall be entitled to sell their cargo on board their vessels without paying any tax, but not to sell from stores or shops in the towns, except on obtaining a burgherbrief. Masters of Danish vessels shall, however, be exempted from taking out a burgherbrief, on paying store tax, according to the provisions hitherto in force. 7. Foreign merchants, or agents of mercantile houses, who arrive in the Islands, shall not be entitled to offer for sale or to sell goods, unless they obtain, in consequence of a petition, which shall be reported on by the policemaster, a license from the Government of the Island, to carry on such traffic with a certain quantity of goods and for a certain limited period, and on paying such a tax to the land treasury, as in proportion to the burthens and tuxes, to be paid by merchants established here, may appear proper ; while the payment to the state treasury and the fee to the police shall be in the same proportion, as directed in 2. 8. The sale of manufactured goods and the like by itinerant sellers shall be restricted to the towns and the Island of St. Johns, and shall be dependent on the grant of a license or pass, issued by the respective policemaster and valid for one month; for such pass $1 shall be paid, which shall go to the land treasury. Such license or pass shall betaken out in the name of the person entitled to carry

on the business, (who, as far as the towns are concerned, shall keep there an open shop) and shall only be used by the person named in the same as seller, with regard to whom it must be observed, that only persons above 35 years of age or individuals, unable from bodily infirmity to perform work of a more laborious nature, are employed as such, with the excep tion of such sellers, who, at least, in the course of the whole last year, before the publication of this ordinance have been constantly employed in carrying about goods for sale. All sellers shall carry their goods themselves, and shall under no pretence whatever lie allowed to take other persons with them for the purpose of carrying their goods. Persons, who, without being provided with a burgherbrief or a license to trade, shall have in the course of the whole last year, before this ordinance comes into operation, gained a livelihood either by carrying about their goods themselves for sale, or by keeping sellers, may be granted licenses or passes for themselves or for one seller, or in case they kept several, for two, on the same conditions as persons entitled to trade. These licenses or passes shall, however, be renewed every month, as hood without intermission ; long as the concerned continue but such a liveli- should any one let 2 months pass, without renewing the license, such pass cannot be granted anew until the concerned has obtained license to trade, and, at the same time, keeps an open shop, but the latter shall not be required in the

Island of St. Johns. The policemasters shall cause lists to be made out and exhibited for public inspection of all persons, to whom this applies, in ihe same manner as directed in 5, with regard to the individuals, mentioned there. 9- No burgherbrief or license shnll be required for a person retailing in his or her dwelling house in the towns : bread, candles, fruits, vegetables, cakes, sirup, sweetmeats, prepared victuals, drinks not containing spirits, eggs, milk, soap, starch, firewood and charcoal, and finally productions of own industry. the In the marketplaces of each town above articles, as well as meat, poultry, fresh butter, meal, pearl barley and other kinds of peeled grain, dry pease and beans, salt and dried fish and salt pork may be offered for sale by country people or others on the usual market day, Saturday or any other day of the week, except Sunday, on which such sale shall be allowed only until 9 o'clock in the forenoon ; and firewood, charcoal, fruits and vegetables

Chap. III. 10. For the exercise of a trade a tax of $18 shall be paid to the landtreasury, in St, Thomas with the addition of one third of the same. Should any one desire to exercise more than one trade, the provisions contained in 3 of this ordinance shall he acted upon, hut with the exception specified below. A burgherhrief entitles the concerned

to exercise his trade to any extent and to employ assistants ns well as to engage apprentices; the latter, however, only on condition, that lie has a fixed residence in the Island and keeps a work shop, if the nature of the trade in general requires such. A burgherbrief as joiner orcarpenteror wheelwright shall entitle the concerned to perform alt kinds of work, which belong to any of those trades; and a luirgherbrief as smith, goldsmith, coppersmith or tinsmith shall entitle to execute all kinds of work in metals. The same rule shall he applicable to other trades nearly connected with one another. A burgherbrief as saddler and painter may he taken out under one without any additional payment, if the concerned previously lias proved his skill or qualification by the performance of a piece of work in each, and either of these trades

shnll be considered as including that of upholsterer. It shall neither tie considered as illicit exercise of a trade, when a master mechanic executes himself in his own workshop or employs in his work place assistants to execute such portions of his work, as else might he considered as belonging to another trade. Whoever has taken out a burgherbrief as mechanic and has settled in any of the Islands, shall lie entitled to exercise his trade in the other Islands, without taking out a burgher -brief there, as long as he does not establish a fixed residence. The widow of a burgher, who, pursuant to the provision of 3 of this ordinance, will continue his trade, shall employ a person, who has proved his skill in the respective trade by the performance of a piece of work, as stated in the following 11. Any one, who will exercise any trade for his own account, shall, after previously having reported this to the policemaster of the place, he bound to perform or execute a piece of work, belonging to such trade, in order to prove his skill in the same, but the choice of the work shall he left to himself. But persons, who have given such proof of their skill in the mother country, shall be exempted from it. Such piece of work shall be executed u der proper control, and shall, when finished, he referred to a committee, consisting of the policemaster and two burghers or ex perl persons. If this committee finds the work properly executed, it shall give a certificate to this effect,

hut it the committee declares, that t lie work executed does not prove, that the concerned is so skilful as a master mechanic ought to be, he can not lie admitted to any new proof of his skill hefore the expiration of half a year. Any mechanic shall he permitted to give such proof of his skill in different trades. F.aeli of the men shall receive for his trouble $ I, and in case it should be requisite to inspect the work in any place out of the towns, moreover, travelling charges, which shall he paid in advance to the policemaster by the person, who desires to execute such piece of work. Whoever has obtained a certificate of having proved his skill shall he entitled to exercise his trade for his own account and to avail himself of the assistance of his wife and children, and the provisions of the preceding regarding the works, that may be executed by the mechanics mentioned therein, shall also be applicable to any one, who has proved his skill as such, but he shall not he permitted to employ other assistants or to engage apprentices, without having previously taken out a burgherhrief. $ 12. No apprentice shall he engaged without a contract in writing, entered into by the muster mechanic and the parents or guardian of the apprentice, which contract shall specify besides the names ot the concerned, the residence of the master and the age of the apprentice 1) The trade and abilities the apprentice shall he taught. 2) The time of apprenticeship, which ordinarily ought not to be shorter

than 3 years. 3) Agreement with regard to the maintenance and abode of the apprentice, or svhat else may be stipulated for him. 4) The payment, the master shall receive for training the apprentice, if any such is agreed upon, as also, on the other hand, the amends the master shall make for non-performance of the contract. The contracts, which may be written on unstamped paper, shall be acknow-

lodged before the policemaster, who shall attend to that they are conformable to the above, and thereafter note them in a protocol, kept for this purpose. If the parties should desire it, such contracts may also be made before the policemaster and entered in the police journal, in which case the parties shall receive each a transcript without payment of any separate fee. A contract of apf>renticeship ed by mutual agreement of the parties, can not be altered or annulunless this is done before the policemaster and entered in the police journal. Either party may demand the contract of apprenticeship annulled, on account of non-performance in essential points, on the part of the other party, or on account of such circumstances as render its continuation impossible or inexpedient. For non-performance of the contract or other improper conduct toward the apprentice, the master shall ordinarily be liable to a fine, and it shall, in this respect, make no difference whether the conduct, on his part, is of such a nature as ought to cause the contract to be annulled or not. Apprentices are subject to correction by the master, and are, moreover, in consequence of a complaint, on the part of the master to the policemaster, liable to proper punishment, according to law. For noting a contract of apprenticeship a fee of $2 shall be paid to the police. 13. Such mechanics, as before the first of October 1852 have exercised a trade for their own account and kept assistant

journeymen and apprentices, shall, notwithstanding the provisions contained in this ordinance with respect to the proof of skill by performance of a piece of work or the possession of a burgherbrief, be permitted to continue their trade as hitherto, but they shall not, without previously having taken out a burgherbrief, for which purpose, however, no proof of skill shall be required, be allowed to engage new apprentices. Persons, who can produce evidence of having before the same period gained a livelihood byexercising a trade for their own account, but without keeping assistant journeymen or apprentices, shall likewise be permitted to continue such trade in the same manner, with the assistance of their wives and children and without proving their skill by the performance of a piece of work. The policemasters shall cause lists to be made out and exposed to public inspection, of all persons, to whom the above provisions are applicable, in the same manner as prescribed by the 5th of this ordinance with regard to the persons mentioned there, whereafter the names of the concerned with the necessary explanations with regard to the trade, apprentices Ac., shall be entered in a protocol, kept for that purpose. Contracts of apprenticeship which may exist before this ordinance conies into operation, but are not made in writing and noted in the police office, shall within three months after the promulgation of this ordinance be adjusted there, ceding but without the payment of any fee, and else be null and void. agreeable to the provisions of the pre- ,

Baking of bread and of cakes shall until further continue as hitherto open to all, unless carried on to such an extent, that it should be thought proper to enjoin on the concerned to take out a burgherbrief, but no proof of skill shall be required in this respect. The same rule shall until further be applicable to the butchery of the smaller animals, but for butchering horned cattle and calves a burgherbrief shall be required, agreeable to $ 4 of this ordinance. IV. 16 Ownership ol vessels is considered as being included in the burgherbrief for carrying on trade by wholesale ; but it is besides the object of a separate burgherbrief, for which a tax of 8 30 shall lie paid to the landlreasury, in St. Thomas with the addition of one third of the same. works belonging thereto a tax of 8(50 shall he paid to t/ie landtreasury in St. Croix, but in the two other Islands 840. Persons, transgressing this ordinance or committing acts, tending to elude its directions, shall be liable to a line of trom 85 to 8100, which in cases of repetition shall be doubled, unless the provisions of the ordinance of this day's date to prevent vagrancy should be applicable, which fine may, however, be reduced to 81, on cause being shownj Goods, illicitly carried about for sale, shall, moreover, be seized and confiscated for the benefit of the landtreasury. The police shall officially attend to, that no illicit traffic, trade or profession is carried on ; but every one, exercising any trade or profession, shall, moreover, be at liberty to inform against any person, guilty of illicit exercise of his trade. For the St. Croix Avis. Shame on the wretch who will not expend a few blank-shots over the grave of a departed antagonist. For ourselves, we might have sometimes assisted in helping an opponent or two out of this indifferent world ; but we have always abhorred every thing like vindictiveness towards the dead. It is, therefore, with unfeigned regret, that we announce to sympathizing absent friends and acquaintance, the demise of the Quashing Principle. This melancholy event happened on Monday last. The blessed defunct up to that day showed so many signs of vigor, that his friends were persuaded he would have survived the crisis. But grim death with his ruthless scythe cut short the threads of his existence, in spite of the indefatigable exertions of his skilful physicians. He as to make the very quadrupeds expired with a yell of pain so terrific shudder. and horrible His mortal remains were conveyed to the grave amid the mingled sorrow and gladness of poor relations and exulting friends. Previous to the commenceheard exclaiming : " Is Mr. Banks present ?" ment of the obsequies, a sepulchral voice was The clever undertaker of smutty memory thereupon stepped forward the type of Andrew Fairservice, stripped by the caterans þÿ or rather looking much like the prototype of Faust. Having duly responded as Master of Ceremonies in a treble equal to that of a gosling, the solemn procession moved on in pell-mell order to the churchyard, where the body was deposited in the family vault. To the astonishment of all present no

funeral oration was delivered by the modern Demosthenes. He was apparently so dumbfounded as not to be able to vent even his feelings in any other manner than by squeaking most discordantly. The quashing principle has been thus laid in the cold grave to await its final account. The surviving friends comfort each other with the assurance, that the void occasioned by the death the dear departed will be duly filled up by " Mr. of Banks !" Ere we bid peace to its ghostly shade, we will permit ourselves to address a few words of condolence to sorrowing relations. The untimely end of the blessed defunct was the effect of his own self-will and stubbornness, united with a disregard of advice, which in this case amounted to a recklessness as uncommon as fatal. Though frequently told, nay begged to desist from the course he was pursuing, the poor man would not be ruled, but persevered in his suicidical attempts until death put a stop to his career. As his death can be imputed to his meddling with matters above his comprehension, it is to be desired that melancholy and " premature" death. the surviving friends will take a lesson from his Rcquiescat in pace I St Thomas, 18th September, 1852 T 0

O." from the spirit of the remarks in his article, appears to be a wonderful adept, not only in detailing, but also embellishing, the gossip of his neighbours ; of telling, and more than telling, such circumstances as really transpired. The facilities which " T. O." hap- would suit his purpose, to make them appear as having cription of persons now vulgarly called tattlers. " T. pens to possess, prepare us to class him with a des- O." further efficiently personifies the character by shewing that whilst he is exceedingly clever in misrepresenting the affairs or secrets of his neighbors, lie well understands how to keep his own. lie has, therefore, been cautious, when treating of the manoeuvres of" the man of the people," to withhold from the readers of the Avis the trickeries of a party ol which he is the great phalanx. T. O. þÿsays We " do not censure them (the Qnashers ?) for desiring a disunion of Coun- cil" ; and yet condemns the " Quashcrs" for resort-

ing to such means as would unequivocally prove how undesirable a union of Council is and must be. The party whom the man of the people represents, made a ticket of three names, not because any one of that number wished to go, but to prevent if possible a ticket being run, which they and all truly liberal parties ought to feel was not the desirable one. The party of " the man of the people," and " the Agitator," held no secret meetings, nor dispatched any little missionaries and emissaries into holes and corners to ferret votes, nor formed any piquet guards around the polling-booth, to interrogate every voter with whom such a liberty could be taken, as to the persons they intended to vote for ; in fact, the man of the people, the agitator, and their party, have been guilty of no other act than proving that a union of Council is ill qualified to answer for St. Thomas, and that her greatest and most vital interest (commerce) cannot be represented there. As the elections have terminated, St. Thomas will be represented by one merchant, one private gentleman, one military chief, and three officials. Fortunate for this Island, that whenever measures connected with commerce may be introduced in the Council, that interest will stand unprotected, by which means the responsibility of injudicious meddling with so gravo a matter to the colony, will fall upon the shoulders of those who have dared to trifle with it. The question is often asked how far the Crystal Palace on Reservoir Square, may be expected to prove a profitable affair. The following calculation is made, by persons largely interested in the Stock, and who are desirous to take, not a sanguine or extravagant, but a just view of the project ; and we believe it will ultimately prove not far out of the way. We assume that the population contained in New York, and a range of country twenty miles about it, is at least One Million. It is in fact, much more. Of this Million, some will visit the Exhibition repeatedly, some only once, some not at all. We suppose it is a very low calculation to say that one third of this whole population will visit the Exhibition, at least once þÿ which is 333,331- Again the floating population of our city, during the Summer months, is per day, al least Thirty Thousand. It is estimated by some good judges as high as Forty-five Thousand. Of this, a large number will Ire more or less attracted by the Exhibition itself and it may be fairly calculated that of the whole number, one fourth certainly will go up to Reservoir Square. This is 7,500 And as the Exhibition is to be kept open at least 150 days, it gives a total number of visits 1,125,000 1 ,458,000 Or One Million and a half of visits. Now take this another way. This is a quarter of the visits made to the Crystal Palace in London, during only 140 days. And the population of New York is very considerably more than a quarter that of London, and our population

vastly more curious, active, locomotive and expensive in their habits, than that of any part of Europe. Test it again in another manner. This gives an average per day of visitors, of 9,720 Now the daily visits in London averaged 43,000 (And it will be recollected that the London Exhibition increased in popularity and attractiveness till the very day of its close. The visitors for the first week numbered only 41,194, and the last they amounted to 478,773), Which gives to our Palace only between one fourth and one fifth of the success of its great Prototype. The Exhibition of the American Institute, usually held at Castle Garden, has three or four thousand visitors a day. It is surely not extravagant to estimate double the number for the Reservoir Square Building. Any way, therefore, this calculation will be found a safe one. Now look at the Financial Results, 1,458,000 visits, at 50 cts., is $729,000 The estimated cost of the Building is, 150,000 Contingent expenses of Frt., Add for short estimate, Insurance, Management . . . . . 100,000 60,000 300,000 300,000 $429,000 Leaving One Hundred and Forty per cent, as the profits of the concern, and the Building on hand, at th« close of the first Season, and with powor to keep open tho Exhibition during tho continuance of tho lea«o.

The Receipts of the London Exhibition were : From Season Tickets £ 67,61® Receipts at the Doors 356,808 Catalogue contract 3,200 Refreshment Contract Retiring Rooms þÿ Washing Places Taking charge of Umbrellas . "31 Profit from Medals struck in the Build- Receipts from the Exhibition ing . £437,699 Subscription from public-spirited of indi- viduals, when the prospects the Enterprise were doubtful 67,399- Total Receipt : £606,098 The nett profits were more than £250,000 1 The Exhibition was open to the Public but 140 days. The price of admission varied, being, for the first two days, one pound. Then, for throe weeks the was five shilling. For the ensuing ton weeks it price was one shilling for the first week, two shillings and sixpence on Friday, four days of the the end of the and hve term, the price was one shilling for the shillings on Saturday. Afterwards, to first of the week, and two shillings and sixpence on 1' riday four days and Saturday. So that for twenty-eight days the price was five shillings, for thirty days two shillings and sixpence, and for eighty-two days one shilling.

The average daily receipts at the doors, and average number of daily visitors, discarding fractions, were as follows On the 5 shilling days . . . £2,187 8,748 persons. On the 2s. 6d. days 2,415 19,320 do. And on the shilling days 2,721 54,420 do. A comparison significant of the value of low prices, and which we commend to the attention of the Directors of the Crystal Palace about to be erected in this city. Another remarkable fact is that the visitors for the first week numbered only 41,194, and on the last week were no fewer than 478,773 ; showing how the public interest went on increasing. This is encouragement for our friends the Directors aforesaid, who have a Charter, aud can keep their Exhibition open as long as may be agreeable to the public and profitable to the enterprise. The total number of persons paying at the doors was 6,286,984 ; and the grand total of persons who visited the building during the one hundred and fortyone days that it was open, including holders of season tickets, exhibitors, and employed persons, was six millions and sixty-four thousand.

Going a-head with a Vengeance. þÿ Within the last quarter of a century we have made great progress in locomotion, hut we were not prepared for the startling proposition of Mr. D. S. Brown, who proposes to reach America in fortyeight hours, and make the voyage to India and back in a fortnight ! Mr. Brown intends to put his theory into practice by vessels of quite different construction to those at present in use, giving them a greater depth of beam. He proposes to make the under surface of the vessel, which is flat, of two inclined planes; the effect of this will be, when the ship is in motion, to raise her whole hull to the surface of the water, thereby removing entirely the resistance at the bows, which is stated to be the great obstacle of her progress, being an illustration of the principle well known to every school boy who has thrown a stone slantingly on the surface of the water, making wliat is vulgarly called a þÿ duck and þÿdrake. By reducing the angles of the inclined plane speed could be added to the vessel, which could be increased from thirty to sixty miles per hour, and a ship so constructed would be as little a flee ted by the ordinary waves of the Atlantic as a Gravesend steam-boat is by a Thames ripple. The hull of the vessel is of a square tubular form ; the deck, bottom, and sides being of great thickness ; and in order to combine lightness with strength, they are intersected throughout with hollow cells or cavities, consisting of a series of central cells,

surrounded by another series of smaller cells; by means of these the weight of the vessel would be reduced to oneeighth of the amount, according to the number of series employed, and still have nearly all the advantages of so lidity ; while the form in which the hull is made gives to it the strength of a tube, enable it 1o be made of almost any length with perfect safety. If water obtains its wonted superiority as a mode of locomotion, the velocity of a steamship might as much exceed that of a railway carriage, as the railway carriage does the steam-ship. Unseen rocks could not endanger a ship whose path was on the surface ; sea sickness could not take place where there was no oscillation ; and the size of the vessel would

waves. In conclusion, Mr. Brown hopes the numerous advantages to be adduced are a sufficient excuse for this attempt þÿ to add another feather to our þÿwing, by projecting a ship worthy of the ocean she is to traverse, and the two worlds she is to unite.

To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis. Sir, 1 perceive that the þÿI ilotboatwhich has been hauled up on the Protestant Quay, for about six weeks ago, is now to be repaired by carpenters from the Brig of War. I beg, through the medium of your columns, to he informed why the work has been given to the abovementioned workmen. Are there no resident shipcarpenters here to he procured? Were there not, then I should consider it quite right to employ the carpenters from the Brig or any other persons ; hut if, as the case really is, there are such workmen here, I consider it unfair that the work should he given to the abovementioned; for in the first instance, those men are provided for in every respect and are not sent out here for the purpose of contracting and performing public work ; which ought in justice to he given to the workmen of the place. I suppose it will be argued that these men work cheaper. It is very evident they can ; for it makes a wonderful difference when a workman is found in hoard and lodging independent of his wages and when he has to support himself and perhaps a large family out of his daily wages without having any other source of income.

According to the Draft to regulate trades and professions in the Danish West India Possessions, it is specified that mechanics will be compelled to take out Burgherbriefs. llovv is it possible that they can do so, when public work which occasionally oilers, is most generally given to military or naval men to perform. If these men (resident mechanics) are to take out Burgherbriefs, are their rights not to be protected ? From this consideration, I think it very unjust, that the abovementioned class of persons should in any way be allowed to take the work which the resident mechanics ought to have ; and hoping that our representatives will take this matter in consideration when deliberating on the Draft named above, and protect the rights and privileges of the natives in general, I remain, Ac. P. R.

To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis. Sir, I perceive there is a bill introduced in the Col. Council, for a stricter observance of the Sabbath, which law is very much wanted here, for I am almost convinced that, there is no civilized country where the Sabbath is so little thought of as in St. Croix. Those who ought to set the example (the higher Order) are the very ones to break it. I have frequently passed the Government's secretary's Office on Sundays, and seen it open sometimes nearly the whole day. Do you not call that profaning the Sabbath? If they do it with impunity, is it to be wondered at, that other people do it also? Evidently what example the higher Order set, the others will follow. R.

W e regret to learn that Yellow Fever of a very malignant character has made its appearance in Barbados, and had already caused much mortality among the inhabitants. On this painful subject, the þÿ West þÿIndian, of the 14th ult. observes : þÿ þÿ The excessively hot and moist weather, which we have had for the last three or four weeks, has brought with it, we regret to say, the Yellow Fever, of as virulent a character as ever has been witnessed by medical men of the longest experience. Originating in one room of the barrack, at St. þÿAnn sin the short space of five days, it has carried off fourteen men and one officer. Immediately on its appearance, the sick were taken into Hospital, the barracks were evacuated, and the Regiment encamped on the grounds of the Naval Hospital, beyond the garrison. These measures appear to have checked the spread of the disease ; for there are no fresh admission into hospital reported this morning. But so long as the wind continues to the southward and we have the same sultry weather, there must always be apprehensions of the spread, or of the return, of the disease. In a recent report on the fever at Martinique, by the medical men attached to the troops, it was observed, that its prevalence depended on the wind, þÿ that the men were seized when the wind blew from the south ; and when it went round to the east or north, the fever left them ; from whence it was inferred, that the spread of it depended on the state of the atmosphere,
and was not under the control of human means ; for persons were liable to its attack in every place, whether situated

3 T WIU A T It 3. 1 in a high or low elevation ; but those in a low situation, and along the sea coast, were more subject than others. þÿ The Fever has not been confined to the garrison, but has shown itself in the town and suburbs as well. It first appeared at the police station, where it attacked several of the men, anti carried off one of them. þÿ It has since disappeared there, but has shown itself elsewhere. It is with much regret we have to mention, amongst its victims, Mr. Benjamin Clairmonte, the youngest brother of the Messrs. Clairmonte, of this island, and Miss Greenidge, a young lady from the country, on a visit to her friends in town.

In our paper of the 6th instant, we briefly alluded to the wreck at Anegada of the American brig Islam, captain Young. S., bound to some port in the West Indies, with meal, flour, oil, packages of merchandize, Ac., and had no sooner struck on the reef than she was boarded by the wreckers from the shore, who immediately commenced their depredations by plundering several valuable packages of the merchandize. They continued by scuttling the puncheons of meal to extract the contents, and made off into the interior with the meal in bags þÿ otherwise the whole of that article would have been saved. The manufacture, according to the specification, is eft'ected by means of cast-iron moulds, the interior of which are the exact dimensions of the common brick ; in this mould a certain quantity of duff, or waste coal, powdered coke, charcoal, or cinders, is placed, and being carbonised, the amalgamated material swells to the exact form required. Ten Rules for the improvement of genteel society. I. Never return a borrowed article until it is sent for. It is the business of every one to look after his own property ; and you should never interfere with other þÿpeople business. s 2 When you borrow a book from a friend, mark your favourite passages with a pencil ; and if you can spare time, write your observations on the margin. This will show, at once, your own judgment, as your friend to form his, and evince your gratitude for the loan. 3. Never pay your bill till recourse is had to law. You will thus have an opportunity of setting an example of obedience to the state, and of causing your creditors to place more value upon their money, everything being prized in proportion to the difficulty of obtaining it. 4. Always give a poor friend a bad dinner, lest the sight of your luxuries should make him discontented. Regale a rich one with a feast ; for you have no right to ask any to forego his comforts for you. 5. When you call upon an editor of a newspaper, say you will trouble him only for a minute, but be sure you stay an hour ; this will show your own consequence, and teach him a proper sense of the value of time. 6. When addressing a public audience, accompany each substantive with at least four adjectives ; and let your words run in triblets, thus þÿ þÿ life is notoriously brief, fleeting, and evanescent ; and when we reflect, ponder, and þÿconsider. By this means, a discourse, excellent as to length, may be got

up with little expenditure of ideas : and we cannot bo too careful of such rare possessions. 7. Ever affect to be near-sighted, that it may bo inferred much study has made you blind. A literary reputation will thus be obtained, at the expence of an eyeglass ; and you will have an obvious excuse for cutting unfashionable acquaintances. 8. Never pay your newspaper accounts at all. The press is useful only so far as it is free ; and how can that be free which is bought with a price? 9. Never praise the writings of another, but indulge much in sneering at .them. You will thus evince your superior fastidiousness of taste, and give your hearers to infer that you could have done much better yourself had you chosen to take the trouble. 10. If your friend is unjustly attacked, remember that a close mouth makes a wise head, and that contradiction but strengthens opposition. Your defence would betray distrust in Providence, whose care the innocent are.

After some remarks on the form and contents of the protocol had been made by the 3rd crownmember, the Council passed over to the order of the day. To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis. Sir, Through the medium of youv paper, I beg leave to make an enquiry of an occurrence that took place at a funeral on Tuesday evening, in this tow-n ; if legal or respectful ? The clerk of the Protestant church was called upon to perform the funeral rites over a child of limited circumstances, and it was observed, that during the preparation for leaving the house there was a seeming haste on the part of the clerk ; and to satisfy him, the corpse was made ready and in rather an unusual manner moved away ; the clerk then entered his carriage, and drove at a slow pace at the head of thc corpse ; an act that has never before been witnessed here. It would bo well, for us to know, if such is the respect, that is only due from clergy or clerk, towards persons, who die paupers. An Attendant. Frederiksted, 17 th Nov. 1852.

For the St. Croix Avis. Having understood that sundry objections have been started to the propriety of allowing itinerant sellers, vending Bread etc. in the country, we beg leave to call the attention of the Colonial Council to this subject. We think that all such objections may be contained in the following : 1. That the country laborers may be tainted by the example of seeing people from town walking in the country apparently idling. 2. That these sellers may be used by thieves in the country to dispose ot sugar, rum etc., which might be stolen in crop time. 3. That the merchants in town may think themselves injured in their trade by such a traffic. These objections we think may be done away with, when the following precautions be taken : Ad. 1. Those persons who keep sellers ought to pay an appropriate tax for the permission ; they will therefore be obliged only to keep thus will give satisfaction, such sellers who their labor can not be called idling. Ad. 2. Sellers who are found out in committing themselves in this way or causing disturbances in the country, ought to be excluded from the list of sellers; thus only honest and quiet ones will remain, which will likewise quiet the minds of those who have the tear mentioned sub. No. 1. Ad. 3. If the persons keeping sellers are made to pay a proportionate tax according to the business they are doing, the merchants can have nothing to complain of. Having understood that a proposal has been made to erect shops in the country, as a lesser evil, we suppose, we beg

leave to remark, that sellers as above shown, under proper restrictions, are no evil, and that the public mind is entirely against such shops. They will only be a harbouring hole for thieves, idlers and the labourers gamblers, and from serve to draw the mind of agriculture to shopping; besides giving opportunity to infringe on the rum shop laws, and thus an injustice to the rum shop keepers who pay dear for their privilege. This we beg to submit to the Colonial Council with reference to the publications in the Avis of the 12th and 16th instant on this subject.

All doubt on the subject has long ceased to exist. France is dc facto an empire. The deliberation of the Senate, the ratification of the people, are mere matters of form. The only delay that may arise will be in the hesitation of Louis Napoleon himself; but all hesitation is now past, he has cast the die, and must run the risk. If I am to credit the latest intelligence from Vienna, some hesitation exists there as to what ought to be done. The declaration of an hereditary empire treaties ot Vienna. It is lation of the is a direct and open eotrue, in his speech at Bordeaux, Louis Napoleon spoke which were anxious that þÿ those powers for peace ; but lie said to preserve peace ought not to push subordinate questions too far. 1 bis is now regarded as a threat. All the channel islands are being strongly fortified. A Paris letter says : þÿ The news of the recent change of Ministry at tion in Constantinople has created the financial as well as a considerable sensa- the political world of Paris principally because the same accounts which brought the news of the Ministerial ciisis stated that it had been occasioned by the refusal of the Porte to ratify the loan concluded a month ago in London and Paris on account of the Bank of Constantinople. Xt is now, however, quite

understood that the rejection of the loan was not the true cause of the crisis, and that it was merely put forward as a pretext. Indeed, the speculators on the Paris Bourse have shown that they were aware of that fact, for the Turkish loan which had fallen to par on Wednesday last, rose yesterday to its previous value. The true cause of the fall of the Grand Visier, Ali Pacha and the appointment of Mehemet Pacha in his stead, is I understand, as follows : þÿ Count Bacciochi as every body knows, left Paris some time since on a mysterious mission from the future Emperor of the French to Egypt and Constantinople. The result of his mission in Egypt has been already announced. The object of his mission to Constantinople was to demand of the Divan the recognition by the Sultan of the rights of the French over Algeria, and also to demand the recognition of France as the protector of the Holy Places. Notwithstanding the mystery in which Count þÿBacciochi smission was involved, its object was allowed to transpire at Constantinople before the arrival of the negotiator. The Russian ambassador apprised the Sultan of what he had to expect ; and the Sultan alarmed at the excessive pretentions put forward by France had recourse to the influence of Russia for support. It is in consequence of this that Ali Pacha who was the representative of the influence of France in the Divan, was obliged to cede his place to Mehemet Pacha, who represents Russian influence. In ordinary circumstances this change in the cabinet would

be considered as implying a total change of policy, but in the present instance this is not the case. In the internal policy of the country there will be no change; for Mehemet Pacha had cordially joined in all the reforms effected since the advent of Abdul Medjid to the throne. But, on the other hand a most important change will take place in the external policy of the Porte, which by this change is placed completely under the influence of Russian diplomacy. Such is the effect of French intriguing at Constantinople. Let us hope that it may not lead to still worse results.

From the þÿI aris Moniteur The Prince has marked the end of his tour by a great act of justice and national generosity þÿ he has restored Abdel-Kader to liberty. This act has long been decided in his mind; he wished to carry it into effect as soon as circumstances should permit him to follow, without any danger to the country, the suggestions of his heart. At present, France has too legitimate a confidence in his strength and his rights, not to show herself great towards a vanquished enemy. In returning to Paris, the Prince stopped at the Chateau þÿd Amboise, and, having seen Abd-el-Kader, informed him of the end of his captivity in the following terms : þÿ þÿAbd-el-Kader I come to inform you of your liberation. Yon are to be taken to Broussa, in the States of the Sultan, as soon as the necessary preparations shall have been made, and you will receive there from the French government an allowance worthy of your former rank. You are aware that for a length of time your captivity had caused me real affliction, for it incessantly reminded me that the government which preceded me had not observed the engagements entered into towards an unfortunate pnemy ; and nothing in my eyes is more humiliating for the government of a great nation than to misunderstand its force to such a point as to fail in its promise. Generosity is always the best counsellor, and I am convinced that your residence

in Turkey will not prove injurious to the tranquility of our possessions in Africa. Your religion, like ours, enjoin submission to the decrees of Providence. But if France is mistress of Algeria, the reason is that God willed it to be so, and the French nation will never give up that conquest. You have been the enemy of France, but I am not the less willing to render justice to your courage, to your character, and to your resig-

3 tl\ nation in misfortune. That is the reason why I consider il a point of honor to put an end to your captivity, having full confidence in your word. These noble words deeply moved tbe ex-Emir. Alter having expressed to bis highness bis respectful and eternal gratitude, be swore on the Koran that he would never attempt to disturb our rule in Africa, and that he would submit, without any ulterior design, to the will of France. Abd-el-Kader added that it would be quite to mistake the spirit and the letter of the law of the Prophet to imagine that it allowed any violation of engagements towards Christians; and , the he pointed out to the Prince a verse in Koran which formally condemns, without any exception or reservation, whoever violates sworn faith, even with unbelievers. In the opinion of all intelligent Arabs, the conquest of Africa is a fait accompli ; they see in the constant superiority of our arms a marked manifestation of the will of God. A loyal and generous policy is the only one that befits a great nation, and France will be thankful to the Prince for having Jollowed it. Abd-el-Kader will remain at the Chateau þÿd Amboiseuntil all the necessary measures have been taken connected with his removal, and his residence at Broussa. Tbe place assigned for the future residence of Abd-el-Kader is not far from the town where Kossuth and some of bis companions were sent after their escape from Hungary. Broussa, which contains a population of about 50,000 souls, Turks, Greeks, Jews, and Ar-

menians, was once the capital of the ancient Bit liynia. Situate on a flank of Mount Olympus, it was conquered from the Greek Emperors in the beginning of the I4th century, when the passes of the mountain had already been left unguarded, and the victorious Orchan, son of Otliman, succeeded, by force or by treachery, in obtaining possession of it.

Attest om at Jorden ei afgiver nogen Nytte eller Indtaegt udstedcs under Eeds Tilbud af Eieren og tvende Borgere i Qvarteret, og attesteres af Qvarteer-Capitainen Huuseiere, hvis Iluse have staaet ledige i 6 Maaneder og derover og som desaarsag forlange Nedsasttelse i Skatterne, have at indsende tilstraekkeligt Beviis for at Huset har henstaaet ubeboet i det angivne Tidsrum. In accordance with the order of the Government the tax commission for St. Croix will assemble on the undermentioned days at 10 þÿo clock a. m., to receive information in writing relating to the taxes for the present year, viz : For the Country : Tuesday the 23rd November for the inhabitants in Westend Quarter and Northside Quarter Letter A, at the Courthouse No. 53 54 in Queens street in Frederiksted. For Frederiksted : On the same day for the inhabitants in Strand street, and Wednesday the 24th November for the inhabitants in Kings, Queens, Princes, Hospitals, New and Fishers streets, Queens and Kings cross streets, Market and Hill streets, at the above mentioned Courthouse. Besides those elucidations, which are required for the calculation of taxes to the State Treasury as well as to the Land Treasury, and which every owner or lessee of houses in and out of town, or ot estates, is bound to give to the commission, the Government considers it requisite at the same time to be informed of the number of laborers on the estates or of other persons residing there as also of the quantity of stock on the estates etc., for which purpose the blank schemes for the tax lists are furnished with columns to contain such information. Owners of estates arc to specify in writing the exact number of acres in cane cultivation and prepared for cane cultivation, or in other cultivation and pasture, or not in cultivation neither being used nor yielding any profit. As to the land that yields no profit, the owner is to produce

a certificate on oath signed by himself and two burghers of the Quarter, and attested as to its correctness by the captain of the Quarter. Owners of houses that have been unoccupied for six months and upwards claiming a reduction in the taxes, are to give satisfactory proof of the house having been vacant during the period stated. Persons neglecting to produce the information, and proof prescribed by tbe regulation in the above shape, time and place, must ascribe to their own neglect all losses resulting therefrom. Blanks for tax lists will do distributed some days previous to the meeting of the Tax Commission and arc required to bo accurately filled out by the concerned, and delivered to the commission on that day, which is fixed on for each street in the towns, and for each Quarter in the country. Tax Commission for St. Croix, the 28iA October 1852. W. Birch. Kaalund. H. Petersen H. M. Keut«ch.

London Times, October IG, 1652. DILV1IAKK. In the sitting of the Chamber of the 8th inst. the President of the Ministry read a Itoyal message relating to the question of succession. It states that the next heir to the Crown having formally renounced his right by a deed of cession executed on the 18th of July, 1851, and the consent of the head of the oldest branch of the Gottop-Holstein family, the Emperor of Russia, having been obtained to the change, it has also received the assent of the great Powers of Europe, Austria, England, France, and Prussia, with Sweden and Norway, by a treaty concluded in London on the 8lh of May last. By this act it is guaranteed that the Danish monarchy shall remain united in its present extent under one sceptre, even though the direct descendants of Frederick the Third iu the male

d » <8 St AT13, line should die out. According to this arrangement the King of Denmark declares his intention, supported by the above-named acts and treaties, to establish such a succession to the throne: the articles of the Law of Succession of 1GG5 are therefore cancelled, from Art. 27 to Art. 40; and as the next heir to the Crown and government of the States of the Danish monarchy the King names his Royal Highness Prince Christian of Schleswig- Holstein-Sonderburg-Gliicksburg and his descendants in the male line by his marriage with the Princess Louise Wilhelmine Frederica Caroline Augusta Julie, by birth Princess of Hesse, according to the right of primogeniture. According to the articles of the fundamental laws of June 5, 1849, the Chambers are called on to give their assent to this regulation of the succession as far as it relates to the kingdom alone; it will afterwards be made valid by a special act of the King for the oilier Stales of the monarchy. The message is dated the 4th ol October. The Second Chamber of Denmark on the 23d passed for a second reading the bill transferring the Customs frontier of the Monarchy from the Eider to the Elbe ; the voles were 79 for the measure and only two against it. Before it is read a second time the bill is lo be referred to a special committee. M. Tscheining spoke support in of the bill, but expressed some anxiety as lo the course the German Confederation might adopt in the question. Holstein being a state of the Bund. He could not agree

with the Finance Minister that they had no reason to apprehend any interference of the Diet in the regulation of the Customs between Denmark and the Duchy. The Diet had no right to interfere, hut it possessed the power ot doing so. The Minister of Finance, in answer lo a question from M. Tscherning, explained the measures that would be taken to repress smuggling on the frontier of the Elbe. þÿ I open Ibid, November 1.

Antiquarian Discovery. þÿ A few weeks ago, in clearing out the ruins of an old chapel at Nuneham Regis, Warwickshire, which had been pulled down, in all but the belfry tower, about 40 years since, we thought it necessary to trench the wiiole space, that we might more certainly mark out the boundaries of the building, as we wished to restore it, in some measure, to its former state. We began to trench at the west end, and came on a great many hones and skeletons from which the Collins hud crumbled away, till, finding the earth had been moved, we went deeper, and discovered a leaden collin, quite perfect, without date or inscription of any kind. We cut the lead and folded hack the lop, so as not to destroy it ; beneath was a wooden collin iu good preservation, and also without any inscription. As soon as the leaden top was roiled back a most overpowering aroniat'c. smell diffused itsell all over the place. Wo then unfastened the inner collin, and found the body of a man embalmed wilii great care, and heaps of rosemary and aromatic leaves piled over him. On examining the body more closely we found it had been beheaded ; the head was separately wrapped up iu linen, and the linen slurt that covered tlie body was drawn quite over the neck where the head had been cut off; the I lead was laid straight with thebodt, and, where tne joining of the neck and head should have b -on, it was tied round with a broad black riband. His hands were crossed on his breast, the wrists were tied with black riband,

and the thumbs were tied together with black riband, lie had a peaked beard, and a quantity of long brown hair, curled and clotted with blood, round his neck: the only mark on anything about him was on the linen on Ins chest, just above whore his hands were crossed ; on it were tlio letters þÿ TB worked in black silk. On trenching towards the chance! we came oil four leaden Collins laid side by side, with inscriptions on each, one contained the body ol Francis, Earl of Chichester and Lord Dunsinure, 1653 ; the next the body ol Audrey, Countess of Chichester, 1652 j another the body of Lady Audrey Leigh, their daughter, 1640; and the fourth the body of Sir John Anderson, son of Lady Chichester, by tier first husband. We opened the coffin of Lady Audrey Leigh, and found her perfectly embalmed and in entire preservation, her flesh quite plump, as if she were alive, her face very beautitul, her hands exceedingly small and not wasted; she was dressed in fine linen, trimmed all over with old point lace, and two rows of lace were laid flat across lier forehead. She looked exactly as it she were lying asleep, and seemed not more than 16 or 17 years old; her beauty was very great j even her eyelashes and eyebrows were quite perlect, and her eyes were closed ; do part of her lace or figure was at all fallen in.

We also opened Lady þÿChichester coffin, s but with her the embalming had apparently failed ; she was a skele-' ton, though the coffin was half full of aromatic leaves. Her hair, was as fresh as if she lived; it was long, thick, and as soft and glossy as that of a child, and of a perfect auburn colour. Ill trenching on one side of where the altar had been, we found another leaden coffin with an inscription. It contained the body of a Dame Maria Brown$, daughter of one of (he Leighs, and of the Lady Marie, daughter to Lord Chancellor Brackley. This body was also quite perfect, and embalmed principally with a very small coffee-coloured seed, with which the coffin was nearly filled, and it also had so powerful a perfume that it filled the whole place. The linen, riband, etc., were quite strong and good in all these instances, and remained so after exposure to the air, we kept a piece of each coffin, and had it washed without its being at all destroyed. Young Lady Audrey had earrings in her ears þÿ black enamelled serpents. The perfume of the herbs and gums used in embalming them was so sickening that we were all ill after inhaling it, and most of the men employed in digging up the coffins were ill also. My object in sending this account is, if possible, to discover who the beheaded man is. The chapel is on the estate of Lord John Scott, who inherited it from his paternal grandmother, the Duchess of Buccleuch, daughter of tho Duke of Montagu, into whose family Nuneham Regis
and other possessions in Warwickshire came by the marriage of his grandfather with the daughter of Lord Dunsmure, Earl of Chichester þÿ Notes and Queries.

Considerable excitement existed at Vera Cruz, in consequence of the receipt of intelligence, that a French squadron would soon arrive to support the French minister in his demands for the payment of the French creditors; also for the liberation of Lamont, the Frenchman, who, it will be remembered, was cast into a prison a short time since. A Spanish war vessel was likewise expected at San Francisco, (Mexico,) to enforce the payment of claims and debts due to the Spanish government. The port of Mazatlan had been opened. The condition of the frontier States was very deplorable, and revolutionary attempts were ol almost daily occurrence.
