New York Herald. Speech þÿol Louis Napoleon at Bordeaux. I accept with eagerness the opportunity afforded aie, by the Bordeaux Chamber of Commerce, for thanking your great city for its cordial reception and its magnificent hospitality, and I am happy, at the end of my journey, to communicate the impressions I have received. The object of my tour, as you are well aware, was to make myself acquainted, by personal observation, with the beautiful provinces of the south, and to ascertain their real wants. It has, however, led to a far more important result. I may say, indeed, with a candor as far removed from pride as from false modesty, that never did a people more directly, more spontaneously, more unanimously, testify a determination to free itself j from all uneasiness respecting the future, by placing in the same hands as heretofore, a power which sympathizes with its feelings. (Applause.) The people has now at last learned to value at their price the false hopes with which it has been cajoled, and the dangers with which it was threatened. It seems, then, that in 1852 society approached its dissolution, because each party consoled itself with the belief that amid the general wreck it might still plant its standard on the floating fragments. (Sensation, and cries of þÿ Vive ; I'Empereur þÿ! ) Now that their eyes are opened to absurd theo- j ries, the people have acquired the conviction that ( those pretended reformers were mere visionaries, j inasmuch as there has always been a disproportion

and a want of consequence between their expedients and the promised result. (Loud applause, and cries of þÿ True, þÿtrue. )At present, the nation surrounds me with its sympathies, because I do not belong to the family of the Ideologists. To promote the welfare of the country it is not necessary to apply new systems ; but the chief point, above all, is to produce confidence in the present, and security for the future. For these reasons it seems France desires a return to the Empire. þÿ( Yes, yes þÿ! prolonged applause þÿ þÿ Vivel'Empereur þÿ/ ) There is one objection to which I must reply. Certain minds seem to entertain a dread of war ; certain persons say the Empire is only war ; but I say the Empire is peace þÿ (sensation) þÿ for France desires it, and when France is satisfied the world is tranquil. These words, uttered in a firm voice, and with strong emphasis, produced a magical effect. Enthusiastic bravos were heard from all sides. Glory descends by inheritance, but not war. Did the princes, who justly felt pride that they were the grandchildren of Louis XIV., recommence his wars ? War is not made for pleasure, but through necessity ; and at this epoch of transition, where, by the side of so many elements of prosperity, spring | so many causes of death, we may truly say, Wo | be to him who gives the first signal to a collision, the consequences of which would be incalculable. f (Long and profound sensation.) I confess, however, that, like the Emperor, I have many conquests to make. I wish, like him,

to conquer, by conciliation, all hostile parties, and to bring into the grand popular current those hostile streams which now lose themselves without profit to any one. (Applause.) I wish to restore to religion, morality, and opulence, that still numerous part of the population which, though in the bosom of the most fertile country in the world, can scarcely obtain the com- j mon necessaries of life. (Sensation.) We have immense waste territories to cultivate, roads to open, ports to dig, rivers to render navi- j gable, a system of railroads to complete ; ire have opposite to Marseilles a vast kingdom , which we 1 must assimilate to Era nee ; we have to bring all our j great western ports into cormection with the Ameri- j can continent, by a rapidity of communication which wi still want; lastly, we have ruins to restore, false gods to overthrow, and truths to be made j triumphant. (Prolonged applause.) This is the sense which 1 attach to the Empire, if the Empire is to be restored. (Cries of þÿ Vice j VEmpereur þÿ/ ) Such are the conquests which I contemplate, and all you who surround me, and who, like me, desire your þÿcountry welfare s þÿ you are my soldiers ! þÿ( Yes, þÿyes þÿ prolonged applause.) - þÿ þÿ»ooo

Willmer and Smith's European Times. Escape of Erencli Political Prisoner's from Cayenne. The Mependanoe of Brussels gives the following particulars of the escape of several French prisoner from Cayenne Wo have received from

iTIi Paramaribo, the chief town of Dutch Guyana, under date of Sept. 20, a letter signed Riboulet, and of which we cannot guarantee the exactitude, as the signature is completely unknown to us ; but the facts that it contains appear to us to be of sufficient interest to be communicated to our readers. The facts arc as follows : þÿ Twelve persons, transported for political offences in the affair of the 2nd December, to the island of the French Guyana, called He de.la Mere, resolved to attempt to recover their liberty. On the 8th of September, at midnight, after the inspection, each of them provided with a small bundle containing a few clothes and a little bread, went to a spot agreed upon on the sea shore. Four boats not guarded were moored at a short distance from the shore. They swam towards them, and getting into one they cut the others adrift, in order to remove the means of pursuit. Without chart or compass they ventured thus upon the ocean. For 24 hours they proceeded under a burning sun, and in the midst of the greatest peril, without a drop of water to quench their thirst. In passing near the Safety Islands they were perceived, and were chased for five hours. The night came on, and the breakers in the midst of which they were obliged to navigate did not permit be to come up with them. It may their pursuers said, therefore, that they were saved by the very danger that they risked. A few hours afterwards they struck upon a sandbank, and but for a high wind that came on with the tide, they would not per-

haps have been able to get clear of the chased the following day they were again bank. On near Sinamary. They succeeded at length in reaching a Dutch port called Brandswacht. At first they were taken for escaped convicts, but they succeeded in making their real position known. The commandant, who is of French origin, then procured for them all the assistance in his power. After passing three days with this excellent man, they were sent to Paramaribo, where they were in the first instance put into prison, but subsequently they were put on board the Dutch vessel the Helding, and in forty-eight hours afterwards they had permission to land. It is from this town, as we have stated, that the letter has been addressed to us by one of the persons who escaped, and we should give it if it were only to tranquillise the families of the persons whose names arc subjoined. The author of the letter speaks in high terms of the kindness which he and his companions received from the Dutch officers. They hope that they will not be given up to the French Government ; the letter even says that they have received the assurance of the contrary in the name of the Dutch Government. The presence in the roadstead of Paramaribo of the French steamer, the Voyageur, inspired them, however, with some uneasiness, and they had communicated their position to the English authorities at Dcmcrara, and also to those of the United States. Such are the facts conimenicated to us, and of which, we repeat, we-cannot guarantee the exactitude. The

letter, besides, gives the names and professions of the twelve persons who have made their escape, and also the departments to which they belonged. They were as follows : þÿ S. Iliboulet, professor, Jura; J. Reusse, merchant, Paris; J. Bidet, landowner, Allier; G. Billiard, ditto, Allier ; Lcmaitre, founder, Nievre ; A. Tournairc, bootmaker, Ardeehe ; J. Brulat, watchmaker, Basses- Alpcs; II. Miaille, seaman, Vauelusc; L. Cadette, ditto, Marseilles; J. Barthelemy, baker, Basses- A1 pes ; Siol, coachmaker, Ardeehe. The Courier du Havre gives an account of the atte mpt to escape on the part of some of the convicts stationed on the Isle du Salut, at Guyana. These islands, it appears, are obliged to procure their supplies of fresh water from the continent, and a schooner called the Cisterne was employed for the purpose. One day, when this vessel was, as usual, about to discharge its cargo, several convicts resolved on the execution of a plot to possess themselves of it, and to sail away. As its crew was very small in number, it is probable that they would have easily succeeded in their design ; but the man-of-war, the Dugueselin, of 80 guns, at anchor in the roadstead, perceived what they were about, and sent several boats against them. The convicts resisted, and force was employed to subdue them. Several of them were wounded ; two were stabbed so seriously by bayonets that they had to be conveyed to the hospital, and died in the course of a short time. An Incident ok a Spanish Bullfight.

For tlie St. Croix Avis. It is a universal complaint at present, that letters which arc sent from here to St. Thomas, and vice versa, do not always reach their address. This can only be caused by the present manner in which letters arc forwarded, namely not through the post but by private postbags. When the letters reach the destined port, they are snatched up by any one, or lay forgotten in the stores. Some say even that letters arc opened by improper persons cither from idle curiosity or worse motives. We would wish very much that a post institution might be erected between this island and St. Thomas, reducing the present high postage to one or two stivers a letter, which would do away with the evil complained of and furnish a not inconsiderable revenue to the treasury.
The þÿ AVIS. Christiansted, Tuesday the 30th of November 1852.

In the curly part of this year, in noticing the steps the Government had taken, by effecting a daily postal communication between ibis town and Frederiksted, we offered some remarks as to letters between this place and St. Thomas; but like many other useful hints, this article escaped the attention of the authorities. We venture again to say that if arrangements were made at the Post Office here, for despatching and receiving letters to and from St. Thomas, by paying a reasonable postage, say 1 or 2 stivers, the public would be benefitted by the measure þÿ hence the evil complained of by our correspondent in toþÿday number s would be remedied.

lion. Edward Everett, the new Secretary of Slate. The appointment by the President, of Mr. Web- Everett, the friend and biographer of Mr. Secroster, to succeed the deceased statesman, as and tary of State, is peculiarly appropriate, will doubtless be acceptable to men of all parties. Mr.

Everett is well known to the American people, having for the last quarter of a century held many important public stations, and acquired the highest reputation, for his superior talents and purity of character. A few reminiscences of his public career may bo interesting to our readers. While at Harvard College as a student, Mr. Everett was distinguished, though very young ; on leaving college he studied divinity, and was ordained and, settled a youthful prodigy, in the Unitarian church. In elegant literature he had no equal of his age, and the public were delighted with his pulpit eloquence. Whenever he reached crowds of the most accomplished, of oth sexes assembled to hear his splendid sermons. These discourses, if, in the opinion of some they had less of vital piety in them than was shown in the sermons of some other men, were distinguished for a puiity of taste and a sweet solemnity that made him delightful to hearers of all creeds. A few years after his ordination he was elected to a professorship in Harvard University. This office he accepted on condition of being allowed to visit Europe, and reside a year or two in Germany. He set out on this tour with all the ardor of a young man panting tor knowledge, and ambitious of surpassing all in his accomplishments. In his absence, lie visited Home, France, and England ; and tarried for some time at Gottingen, becoming quite enamored with German literature. He extended his visits to Greece, and there drank inspiration

among the relics of ancient taste and grandeur. He returned to his alma mater with a mind tilled with þÿ the spoils of þÿtime, and a memory stored with the humanities þÿ the great object of his travels. He then commenced his labors as a professor, and at once became the pride of the University and the delight of his pupils. At this time he gave a splendid course of lectures on architecture, which was numerously attended by the most enlightened ot both sexes in Boston and vicinity. As principal editor of the North American Review , for a time, he also acquired much reputation, and elevated that periodical to the first rank among reviews. His portions of the work are marked by taste, talent and learning. In short, Mr. Everett was a scholar by profession ; and by many it was considered an evil hour for American literature when the politicians of his district turned their eyes upon him as a candidate for Congress, and induced him to accept a Domination. In 1824, Mr. Everett was elected to Congress from the district in which Cambridge is situated. He resigned his Professorship in college, and took his seat in the House of Representatives, in December, 1825. He was continued by the people as their representative for ten years, and finally left the Halls of Congress in 1830. In the autumn of that year, he was elected Governor of Massachusetts; and being three times re-elected, held that high office until January, 1840, when he was succeeded by lion. Marcus Morton, who was elected over Mr. Everett and all others, by

one vote, in consequence of the odium of the fifteen gallon law þÿ a sort of Maine liquor law. of the þÿ As a representative in Congress and Governor Old Ilay þÿState, Mr. Everett sustained the expectations ol his friends, evincing great talents as a debater and legislator in Congress, and eminent ability as an executive officer, in directing and controlling the affairs of a sovereign State ot the American Union. On the accession of John Tyler to the Presidency, mainly, it is said, through the influence of Mr. Webster, thou Secretary of State, Mr. Everett, in 1841, was appointed Minister Plenipotentiary to Great Britain. It is not too much to say that the important diplomatic affairs of this countiy with that government, have never been entrusted to more able and skilful hands, and novel have those high duties been performed more acceptable to the American people, and received with more favor by the English, than in the case of Mr. Everett. He was recalled by Mr. Polk, in 1845, when ho was succeeded by Hon. Louis McLane. Soon after his return to the United States, ®fr; Everett much University, was elected President of Harvard to the gratification of the friends of literature ; but he did not long continue to hold the office, which he resigned, and was succeeded by Professor Jared Sparks. The speeches and addresses of Mr. Everett form an elegant contribution to by American liters- have been collected and edited himself. They ture. But the most important of his recent lite-

rary labors, is the part lie has performed in editing the works of his friend, Daniel Webster, in six volumes, to which, also, he contributed a biographical sketch of that lamented statesman. It is hoped, by his friends, that he may be induced to undertake the writing of a more elaborate biography of Mr Webster, as no one so well knew

It is a fact worthy of particular note that on the same day in which the severe earthquake occurred at St. Jago de Cuba, there wore unusual eruptions and an earthquake at Mount /Etna. The Malta Mail describes the perils of a party of gentlemen and ladies, who wore ascending /Etna on the night of August 20. The party consisted of Captain and Mrs" Hallett, two Misses turnkey, Hon. Lieutenant Finch (68th Light Infantry;, and Lieutenant Ravenhill, (Royal Engineers), with three guides, three muleteers, andasei vaut, together with 1 1 mules. They left Nicolai at 8 p. m. on the 2 th of August, and arrived at the Bosbo at 11 o'clock, where they found a high wind blowing from the westward. Ascending from thence some two miles, the huge crater below /Etna, called the Colossi, was found to be unusually active, belching forth large bodies of lire and smoke ; and immediately after, /Etna itself began to vomit forth fire and ashes. The weather continued to increase in coldness, until a terrible hurricane burst on the travellers, sweeping them, and the very mules they rode, before it. Follow ing this came an earthquake, which shook the ground under their feet, and filled the guides and the whole parly with consternation. The hurricane, too, continued, and even increased in violence, and the mules were at length abandoned to their fate, while the company pursued their way on foot, and finally reached Nicolai in safety at 10 þÿo clock the following morning. Now, it will

be remembered that the severest shocks of the disastrous earthquake at Cuba, occurred on the afternoon and night of the 2Uth of August, and early on the 21st. The JJi trio de la .Marina, the official journal of Havana, states that þÿ the city of Santiago de Cuba was visited on the 2Jth by a terrific earthquake, unequalled for ils disastrous ravages in the recollection of the oldest inhabitants. The most violent shocks were felt at halfpast 3, p. m. ; thirty minutes after 3 p. m., 9 p. m., 1 a. m. Another very violent one at 3; a. m. ; another at 4 a. m. ; when the atmosphere became very dark, contributing much to increase the ahum. Next day, weather daik, rainy, ami exhibiting a most appalling þÿaspect. From these two accounts it would seem tj be a reasonable inference that the convulsions on Mount /Etua wore connected with the earthquake at St. Jago. þÿ Boston Traveller.

From Beirout to the cedar groves it is three þÿdays journey, and there are two principal routes between which the traveler has to choose. The other follows ing the sea-shore to the northward for a the traveler many a fine prospect of the day, affordsea, as the mule track which he ibllows winds along upon the margin of the beach, or passes over some lofty promontory. Whichever route he takes, the preparations for a journey of several days among mountain passes so rugged and wild, forms usually a very exciting scene. For as there are no inns in these regions, and no accommodations of any kind for the use of travelers, those who journey must take with them clothing þÿ their almost every thing that they expect to þÿ dwellings even, as well as their food and so as to be entirely independent of the require population of the country, in every emergency which may occur during the tour. The Tenth Meeting. The 10th meeting was held on Friday the 5lli November; absent was, on account of illness, the 3d member for Frederiksteds district. The discussions were, on account of no further committee reports having in the meantime been submitted to the Council, limited to an investigation of the question, which might be the proper term for the ultimate closure of the present session, in which respect various opinions were uttered; at last the Governor, in virtue of the 23rd $ of the Colonial Law, determined, that an extraordinary session of 3 weeks from date should he granted. The meeting was closed at 12 þÿo clock, the next one to be held on Wednesday, lot li instant.

The Eleventh Meeting was held on Wednesday, lOtli November. The Chairman communicated, that lie from divers members bad received the following bills : 1, From the 1st member for Frederiksted district : a proposition regarding indemnification to lie granted to the estate of the deceased Judge Audresori, to Police Assistant Ditlriclisen and Merchant Win. Moore, for ibe losses inflicted upon them during the negro insurrection. 2, From the same member: a bill, signed by divers planters, regarding

the immigration of labourers from other countries. 3, From the 3tl member for Cliristiansted district : a liill proposing a partial alteration of 25 of the Colonial Law, as far as regards the words : þÿ the meetings of the Council are not þÿpublic. 4, From the 3 1 member for St. Thomas district : a hill containing a comparative statement of the import duty on articles of provison, on the manner said duty has hitherto been imposed, and as it is now, according to the law of30th June 1831), also recommending a reduction or a more equalized division of this part of the duties, namely as regards articles of luxury, imported from foreign places. The Council then passed over to the 1st reading of the draft on the country school regulations; the Governor admitted, that the report of the Committee contained propositions of sundry alterations, which would tend to improve the law, hut that he, however, could not agree to all of them. The Speaker of the Committee, 3rd crown member, explained the motives, which had led to the proposed alterations, and the 1st member for St. Johns dwelt on certain points regarding his own district, particularly the Sunday schools. The Chairman declaring, that this 1st reading was closed, the message from Government regarding the revision and decision of the Landlreasury accounts was read for the 1st time. Also the hill proposing a tax to he imposed on horses and boats in St. Johns, was brought to the 1st reading. The mover, the 1st member for the said dis-

trict, introduced and recommended it the Council, on account of tin nl.solut,. strenuously to the particular attention of was held on necessity to procure means tor the Land treasury of that island. Lastly the hill proposing the establishment of a Board of Commerce at St. Thomas, was put under preliminary discussion. The mover, 3d member tor St. Thomas, proposed, and supported by the 3rd crown member, that the Council would adopt this hill as its own, and strongly recommend it to the special care ofGovernment ; it was resolved that the matter should he made over to the 1st reading.

If words convey any ideas at all, we think that the 25th paragraph of the Colonial Law conveys this : that the proeedings of the Council shall as speedily as possible bo published. From the connection of this sentence with the one preceding, it appears that such publication is designed as compensation for the priviledge of an Assembly open to the public, of which we are deprived. Consequently this publication should be made as speedily as possible, to make up for this disadvantage in the Colonial Law. How astonished must we not therefore be, to see such an open violation of this law, when, for example, the proceedings of the Council on the 2Uth October, are first publi-hed on the 30th November þÿ Is this þÿ as Out i lion i li ami a day later! soon as possible. þÿ? Where does the honorable Chairman, to whom tho publiontiou of the proceedings, at one of the 1st meetings was referred, find authority for such conduct ? Can he justify himself, on the ground that the business of the Council, left no time for the preparation of the extract ? We hope notþÿ for the public can never be satisfied with such an excuse. This publication, as long as it is so distinctly laid down in the law, cannot be considered as a secondary m itter, to be left for performance during leisure. Such con luet reminds us too strongly of that ancient regime under which we have unfortuto see abandoned. n itely too long þÿsuffered and which we now hope W bon we fiul tho Government declaring, that we ought n ot to be deprived of the freedom of the

press, as an important means of diffusing knowledge of th j actual state of things, and of the defects under which the state of society is labouring þÿ wo must enquire, how can public opinion be known on subjects of such great importance, as the laws which arc to regulate society, even if we be granted, as we suppose we will, the freedom of the pressþÿ if such subjects are to bo discussed (by our own representatives too !) so privately, that when we do hear of them þÿ the discussions arc already closed ? Our representatives, were they even as wise as Salon, could still never be the less wise, (if they are not ben efited ) , from the free interchange of opinion. Why, therefore, deprive us of tho means of giving our opinion on such important subjects which so closely concern us all, by keepiug us in ignorance of them ? When we receive the publication of the proceedings of the C mncil, one month alter their occurrence, it is then totally useless to make any rein i ks which we may find ourselves inclined to do. A free press, therefore, as far as the Council is concerned, could certainly under these circumstances be of no use. H.

The statement of various grievances set forth in the document produced before the þÿ Colonial þÿCouncil and which caused an unfavourable demonstration, was never intended to be brought forward in that informal manner. " petitions and complaints from private individuals The 5th of the þÿ Colonial þÿLaw states, that Ought to be referred to the King or the proper þÿauthorities, and cannot be received by the Council þÿ unless a member adopts such representation as his own þÿ; therefore, the parties concerned, committed an error in directing their hasty sketch to the Representatives for Frederiksted, whose duty it was, nevertheless, previous to its presentation to have revised the same by condensing the þÿ grievances complained of in the form of a þÿBill, wherein no objectionable allusions would have been found in regard of any person or individuals. At the time of the drawing up of this document, it appears that there existed considerable doubts, as to that degree of attention which the subject would receive, together with the false impression that no complaints from a class considered hitherto as unprotected, would be noticed by a majority of the members of Council, unjustly charged with the unfounded supposition that þÿ entirely absorbed in the eagerness to advance their selfish views, they would neglect the welfare and interest of that community whom they are in duty bound to þÿprotect. sions in regard of this affair ; the question before the House was the irregular manner in which the document was brought forward, also, the objection 1 of some of the members against the introduction of charges of a personal nature, when unassumed by any of the members in the manner specified in to the unprotected class þÿ the 5th The Council did not neglect the attention due þÿ. þÿ we deny that such a class exist in the Danish Westindia Colonies. þÿ The Representatives the whilst admitting from Frederiksted, ahd others, memorial from the parties in West End to be out of order, nevertheless earnestly, urged its þÿ reception, and on one of the members adding that he assumed the þÿdocument the House, eventually, acceded to the proposal, and it was read with the omission of all personal allusions. The matter has, subsequently, been decided in such a manner, as to conve y to the parties connected with the memorial, the conviction that the Representatives of the Danish Colonies during the 1st session of the Colonial Council have, notwithstanding the arduous task devolving upon them, faithfully and zealously performed their duty to their constituents, to the community at large, and ; the Government! When the King, without any solicitation on the part of the colonists, established such an institution as the Colonial Council, no

It is supposed that the vessel had about $0,000,000 oil board, which was sent by the home government to pay off troops in her dominions in the new world. Submarine Navioation. þÿ A new diving boat of a most ingenious character, has been recently invented in France, and is now to be seen at Cherbourg. The inventor, Dr. Paverne, has not only discovered means to descend to the bottom of the sea, and to work there at his ease with a body of operatives, audio remain there as long as lie pleases, replacing by chymicnl proceedings the oxygen absorbed, but lie has discovered a mode of directing the boat under water hy steam, as it it were on the surface. He has engaged to start from any harbour in France and to reach the coast of England, although navigating under water. Mr. Ducoa, the Minister of Marine, on his recent visit to Cherbourg, gave a most friendly reception to M. Lamiral, the partner of Doctor Paycrne, and, having examined the boat, 'promised to introduce the discovery of sub-marine navigation to the notice of the Prince President.

One seldom meets with a truer thing than the following observations by a quaint and witty author upon termed, less hy way of " eminence," what are perhaps, þÿ Talkers'. "Great Talkers not only do rather than "notoriety," Gral the least, but generally say the least, if their words be weighed instead ot reckoned. He who labors under an incontinence of speech seldom gels the better ol his complaint ; for lie must prescribe for himself, aud is very sure of having a

fool for his physician. Many a chatterbox might pass for a shrewd man, if he would keep Ins own secret, and put a drag-chain now and then upon his tongue. The largest minds have the smallest opinion of themselves ; fortheir knowledge impresses them with humility, hy showing them the extent of their ignorance, and the discovery makes them taciturn. Deep waters are still Wise men generally talk little, because they think much. Feeling the annoyance of idle loquacity in others, they are cautious of falling into the same error, and keep their mouths shut when tlicy can not open them to the purpose. The smaller the calibre of the mind, the greater the hue of' a perpetually open mouth. Human heads are like hogsheads þÿ the emptier thev are, the louder report lltey give of themselves. I know human specimens who never think ; they only think tlicy think. The clack of their word-mill is heard, even when ihere is no wind to set it going, and no grist to come from it. A distinguished Frenchman, of the time of Cardinal Richelieu, being in the ante chamber of that wily statesman, on one occasion, at the time that a great talker was loudly and incessantly babbling, entreated him to lie silent, lest lie might annoy the cardinal. " Why do yon wish me not to speak?" asked the chatterbox; "1 talk a good ileal, certainly, bill then I talk well." " Half ol that is true !" retorted the sarcastic Frenchman.

The disgusted Wife to her Husband. " Yon promised to leave off your smoking, The day I consented to wed ; How little I thought you were joking, How fondly believed what you said ! Then alas ! how completely you sold me, With blandishments artful and vain j When you emptied your snuff-box, and told me You never would fill it again I " Those fumes so oppressive from puffing, Say, what is the solace that flows ? And whence the enjoyment of stuffing A parcel of dust in your nose 1 By the habits be you no thus are pursuing, There can pleasure conferred ; How irrational, then, is so doing þÿ Now, isn't it very absurd ? " Cigars come to threepence each, nearly, And sixpence an ounce is your snuff; Consider how much, then, you nearly, Must waste on that horrible stuff! Why the sums In tobacco yon spend, love, The wealth in your snuff-box you sink, Would procure me of dresses no end, love, And keep me in gloves þÿ only think ! " What's worse, for your person I þÿtremble Tis going as fast as it can ; Oh ! how should you like to resemble A smoky and snuffy old man ? Then resign, at the call of affection, The habits I can not endure; Or you'll spoil both your nose and complexion, And ruin your teeth, I am sure !" Whatever may he said of smoking-, it must he admitted to havebeen the cause of much pleasant writing; nor has it failed to be turned to profitable instruction in verse; as witness the lines on a pipe : " The pipe that is so lily white, In which so many take del-ght, ' Tis broke by the touch,

Man's life is but such þÿ Think of this when you're smoking tobacco !" Who is the author of these " Refections of a Tailor ?" It is one of the best things of the kind we ever saw. Nothing can be more happy than the manner in which all the chief implements and materials of " the craft" are introduced ; il Day bath put on joolrM., and around His burning bosom buttoned it with stars. Here will I lay me on the velvet moss, That is like padding to earth's meagre ribs, And hold communion with the things about mc. Ah me ! how lovely is the golden braid That hinds the skirt of night's descending robe : The twin-leaves, quivering on their silken threads, Do make a music like the rustling satin As the light breezes smooth their downy lap. Ha ! what is this that rises to my touch So like a cushion ? Can it be a cabbage ? It is, it is, the deeply-injured flower, Which boys do flout with ; but yet I love thee, Thou giant rose, wrapped in a green surtout ; Doubtless in Eden thou didst blush as bright As these thy puny brethren ; and thy breath Sweetened the fragrance of the spicy air ; But now thou scemest like a bankrupt beau Stript of his gaudy hues his and sober And growing portly in essences, clothes. 1 Is that a swan that rides upon the water ? Oh no I it is that other gentle bird Which is the patron of our noble calling I well remember, in my boyhood's time, When these young hands first closed upon a goose : I have a scar upon my thimble-finger Which chronicles the hour of young ambition.

My father was a tailor, and his father, And my great grandsire : all of them were tailors. They had an ancient goose of ; our From some remoter tailor it was an heir-loom race. I am not certain, hut I think 'twas he Who through misfortune was unfortunate. No matter ; 'tis a joy to straighten out One's limbs, and leap elastic from the counter, Leaving the petty grievances of earth, The breaking thread, the din of clashing shears, And all the needles that do wound the spiWt ." That is a beautiful superstition which prevails When dians. among the Seneca tribe of In- an Indian maiden dies, they imprison its young of bird until and it then begins to try power song, a first loading it with kisses and caresses, they loose its bonds over her grave, in the belief that it will not fold its wings, nor <;lose its eyes, nntil it has flown to the spirit-land, and delivered its precious burden of affection to the loved and lost. It is not unfretjuent to see twenty or thirty biikl s fet loose over a single grave.

THE COLONIAL COUNCIL! CLOSE OF THE FIRST SESSION ! twenty-third sitting, 30th November 1852. Speech of His Ex. Gov. FEDDEItSEN, tfc., Sfc., Sfc. The following statement, connected with the close of the first session of the Colonial Council, will supply to a certain extent, that portion of information, demanded by the public. In the following report of His þÿExcellency a s ddress to the Council will be found sentiments, which could not fail to produce a forcible and lasting impression on the minis of the members ; and which, when published, will be received with respect and esteem. On that interesting occasion, the dignity of the office, and character of the nation was fully maintained. Such a result was not only desirable but also in accordance with the unquestionable fact, that throughout the session of the Colonial Council, the greatest decorum has been maintained. There exists no authority to deny the tribute due to the character of the Council þÿ no public Assembly could lay claim to a higher degree of order and parliamentary courtesy, superior to that which has been happily maintained in this instance þÿ þÿ moreover, in adverting to this interesting feature, it is proper to state, that the various interests of the different communities have been fitly and firmly defended, in that manner, as to convey to the Home Government a correct opinion of the ability and independence of the members, and that, which is equally estimable, the patriotism and national character of the Council.

Public curiosity and right demands loudly, What has been done by the Colonial Council ? There can be no difficulty in replying thereto, and that in a triumphant manner. After a laborious task the result proves, that much has been accomplished þÿ a noble mission has been performed. In the presence of conflicting interests ; in the presence of hostile elements, it has been the good fortune of the Council to accomplish an important duty. Among its labours, the Colonial Council could not remain inactive or betray any apathy in regard of one of the valuable interests of these Colonics. Next to the agricultural interest, that of the mercantile body has been steadily sustained ; and in the language held in the Council, responded to by the worthy representative of the Government,

8 T <© 'Ji 3 ATIS» will be found the guarantee, that the communal interest of these Islands will be fully supported. With these convictions the necessity of uniin , of mutual co-iperaticn is self-evident ; without which no public undertaking or local amelioration can be secured. The mechanical interest has been also supported, and it is not necessary þÿ it would be superfluousþÿ to add, that the most serious attention has been given in behalf, and in advocating the interest, of the poorer classes. On this theme, there could exist no difference of opinion ; the unanimity of the Council on that vital question, will, it is presumed, produce beneficial effects on the future sittings of the Council. Humanity demands not only a prompt and energetic co-operation with the Government, with the view of alleviating the condition of the unfortunates ; but that share of activity and prudence in the framing of equitable laws, to guard against any additional burthen beyond those under which the inhabitants now, unhappily, labor. Extraordinary occasions demand extraordinary efforts þÿ with the exception alluded, there can be no doubt as to the result ; Governor Feddersen has declared in Council : þÿ þÿ That in all matters concerning the welfare of the poorer classes, the Government and the Council will be always þÿunited. These sentiments will be remembered. Society demands that the qualifications of the mind will correspond with those of the heart ; and when it is found, that the union is perfect, we acknowledge

the power of the individual to confer on his fellow citizens that share of relief demanded by circumstances. Will it be refused ? No ! reason forbid the thought. We are reluctantly compelled to subscribe to the fact currently stated, that the various communities are, to a certain extent, at this moment, ignorant of the amount of labour or usefulness performed by the Council. It is, therefore, necessary to add, that ere this, it is supposed that valuable information has been forwarded to the Home Government the mist, if any, will soon be þÿ dissolved ; and we have the strongest reason to of information now established, and the princi- augur the most is favorable results. The medium pal object and purpose of the Danish Government, in establishing the Colonial Council is secured þÿ namely, that organ through which a faithful and efficient representation of the grievances of the lnhaDUaius win De orougnt to the notice of His Majesty, and thereby obtain the necessary relief. The first session after the 23d sitting of the Colonial Council was closed on T uesday the 3uth November 1852. At half past ten the members assembled, but with the usual restlessness to be observed on the eve of the close of all public assemblies, divided into groups, on whose countenance could be easily distinguished the evidence of anxiety, impatience, regret gaiety. or The various reports were then read, at the conclusion of which His Excellency the Governor in full dress entered the Council Hall from the western entrance, and immediately

ascended his seat on the platform. The members after having saluted His Excellency, took their seats. After a temporary silence, His Excellency rose and in a distinct manner addressed the Council in danish. The speech was delivered with all the all self-possession, which offers a great advmtage to in a such public demonstration, when united commanding person and full tone of voice. Having concluded His Excellency resumed, and addressed the Council in the following terms : Gentlemen ! The moment has at length arrived when it is my duty to close this first session, which has occupied, almost, the period of two months. Allow me to say, that it would be unjust to have expected from this Assembly, that which would be looked for from an Assembly, long established, and among whom the members were perfectly acquainted with each other þÿ such could not be expected from a new Assembly and new members exposed to many difficulties. þÿ I am, nevertheless, happy to be able to state, that in the result of the discussions, you havo shown a large share of ability, personal qualifications, and good will, united with the strongest desire to promote all matters in due form ; not only in the verbal discussions before the House, but also in the different committees þÿ all of which will be carefully placed to the notice of His Maþÿjesty Government. s þÿ You return, Gentlemen ! and I trust will experience the conviction, that you have produ-

ced by your useful labours the most gratifying duty to your gracious Sovereign þÿ the framing of just and equitable laws þÿ for which, Gentlemen, accept my thanks and grateful acknowledgment. It is also a part of my duty to express my esteem and personal regard for the gentleman in whose hands you have placed the charge of Leader of this Assembly, and my admiration of his courteous deportment and the efficiency shown by him, as well as my acknowledgment of the services of the Honorable Vice Chairman and those of the Honorable Secretary, in the discharge of his difficult task and functions throughout the session. I will now conclude by repeating the assurance of the sentiments already expressed, and have the honor to declare, in His þÿMajesty name, s the first session of the Colonial Council þÿclosed. The style and delivery of this addiess could not fail to produce a profound emotion on the members, who, with a spontaneous burst gave vent to their loyal sentiments in the unanimous cheer of GOD SAVE THE KING ! !

A FIRE broke out about half past eleven þÿo clock on Tuesday night, the 7th instant, in the town of Frederiksted. On the alarm being given, the people rushed out of their dwellings, and discovered the rooms in the yard of the house No. 9 Strand Street, entirely enveloped inflames. The Engines of the Garrison and the Brand Corps, were prompt in attendance, and with the assistance of the inhabitants, who exerted themselves in a praiseworthy manner, the fire was extinguished at about 1 þÿo clock. The rooms, which were unoccupied, were burnt to the ground þÿ the dwelling-house on the premises, occupied by Mr. Thomas J. Armstrong, received but little injury, the kitchen also received but little injury, and the adjoining house, l clonging to Mr. R. G. Knight escaped with trifling injury. The conduct of the women, as on former occasions, was excellent, þÿ they worked well in supplying water to the engines. þÿ It is not known how the fire originated.

The Speaker of the Committee, the 1st member for Frederiksteds district, as well as its Chairman the 3rd crown member, gave the requisite elucidations with regard to questions, whether it would of be this advisa- ble to extend certain $s. law, whether both of the or only $9 should be extended, whether 8 was considered applicable in regard of the National Church, or only the other acknowledged Churches. This first discussion being closed, the filli member tor St. Thomas district proposed, on account of the limited time and the great quantity of work which was yet at hand, that the Council should resolve, that no more private bills should be received during this present session, at any rate that they should only In read. This proposal met with opposition on the part of several members, add to which thcehairni in declared, that, although it certainly was not desirable that more private bills should he produced, vet, on account of that free excess, which the 5th $ of the Colonial Law

afforded to produce such bills, he could not take upon himself any general compulsion to reject them. The question was however not brought to t lie vote, it being acknowledged as a matter of course, that such bills, which time would not allow being discussed upon and this would have to remain undecided upon until a following session. 'Flic 17th meeting being fixed for Monday the 22nd and the order of the day for the same made known by the Chairman, the meeting was closed at 2 þÿo clock. The Seventeenth Meeting AVas held on Monday the 22nd November. No. 1 on the order of the day, the 2nd discussion of the draft on the Budget for 1853 and 54, was finally concluded. No. 2 tile 2nd discussion of a bill recommending the establishment of a Board of Commerce in St. Thomas, in consequence of which the mover, 3rd member for St. Thomas district, read a letter from a considerable number of Merchants in St. Thomas, recommending the same. It was agreed upon with 15 votes that the proposal of the mover: that the object of the bill he strongly recommended to the care of the Government. of the law of 1 3i li April 1851. TJi« nn-t-iins vas closed at 3£ þÿo clock. The Nineteenth Meeting was held on Thursday the 25lh November. The 3rd member for Christiansted was absent. For the St. Croix Avis. To the Honorable Counsellor Kunzen, Chairman of the Colonial Council. Sir, þÿ At the close of the first session of the Colonial Council, and on the eve of my departure from the Island, it is a duty incumbent on me, auJ I mum lire task with unmindful satisfaction, to express the high sense I entertain of the courteous and gentlemanly deportment maintained by you. during the discharge of your duties as Chaiini in of the said Council. Permit me to add the hope, that in the conviction of the important results, which are looked for from the farther exertions of the Members connected with the late proceedings, that you will continue your valuable and zealous efforts to secure these results, and thereby advance the interests of the Government, the welfare of the different communities, and particularly the relief of the poorer classes. I have the honor to be, Sir, Respectfully, your obedient servant, Joseph De Gout, Mem. Col. Council. 30th November 1852.

Fob the St. Croix Avis. The annual examination of the pupils at the Danish School, took place on Friday last. We regret to say, that there was a decided decline in aim ist all branches, compared with the preceding years. There were only two boys, in the upper class, who distinguished themselves in reading and translating from the danish. We noticed no examination in Danish Grammar ; the fact is, we were led to understand, that although some of the scholars have expressed a desire to study danish giammar, they have met with no encouragement from the teachers. The remarks on the falling off, in point of improvement, apply piineipally to the far so-called danish department ot the school. As as the objects ol the Lancasteiiun school are concerned, the pupils showed some advancement. And in speaking of the defects to of the school, course, be understood exclude the department we must of of uubioidery and needle-work; which reauires no itmaiks of ouis in commendation, such being so gene tally bestowed, in the community, on the conductress of this department, as not to make it necessary to say anything here on the subject. We mean therelore, to confino our remarks to the upper class, which from the name, one would suppose to be in advance of the others ; and in which mole advanced iustiuct ion is given. But beie we must beg leave to state, that with one or two exceptions, viz : a compendious History of the World and Drawing þÿ tho subjoota taught in

this class, in our opinion, are those which strictly belong to The classes. þÿ þÿChambers Geographical other classes less advanced than upper subjects taught are these þÿ s þÿPrimer intended : by the publishers for or primary of children about six seven years old ; schools composed Arithmetic þÿ the children not being further advanced than Ilule of Three ; þÿ þÿMurray Simplified s A small Danish Geography ; and A dogmatical little catechism. If these are subjects for upper classes, we feel ourselves unable to determine what should be taught in the lower classes. Such simple education, or rather instruction, for we cannot consider ourselves warranted to call mere reading and writing education þÿ since they are only means, without which we can learn nothing, but which contain no learning in themselves þÿ such instruction we must declare to be insufficient, considering the large expense of $ >50 monthly, which the public are obliged to defray for the school in this town and the one in Frederiksted. With regard to the latter, we have been informed, whether correctly or not, we have no means to determine, that no parents having any desire for the moral and intellectual cultivation of their children, would think of sending them there. Accordingly, while the teachers continue to receive their very fine salaries þÿ the school is attended by very few children : parents preferring to send them to private schools. We, for our part, must consider that for this outlay, $550 monthly, a higher quality of instruc-

tion should be expected. Where would be the difficulty for teachers, who are willing to work for the pay which they get, to give instruction to a high class in such subjects as : Kuglish and Danish Composition and Grammar, History, Mathematics <5c. Such an extension of the objects of the school would raise it to some degree of respectability, and would prevent the necessity of parents sending their children to other countries ; (except in cases where a more general education is desired ) where, without having any one to inspect their progress, they are entirely neglected. Another subject to which we beg leave to call the attention of the school commission, is the manner in which the examinations are conducted. The teachers are the examiners, while the commission sits and observoo tho proficiency of Uic pupil. Now, it is evident, that for the þÿteacher s own reputation, he will take care to examine a pupil only in such subjects as he has made some of progress in, and perhaps even in certain parts a book which the pupil has attentively studied for this purpose. Under such circumstauces, the commission and visitors must be deceived by false appearances as to the progress of the scholar. We would suggest þÿ that a class should bo brought up before the commission. The teacher should then state what subjects they have been taught. The commissioners should theu select at random from the school books some portion which the scholar shall rehearse or explain, as the case may be. Such a method of examination, we are fully

persuaded, from having tried the plan with a few of the scholars, would cause the school to appear in its true light þÿ and would show even a lesser degree of advancement, than it appears to have arrived at. B. Christianstcd, 13th December 1852.

Mr. Printer, þÿ Will you or any one else have the goodness to explain by what authority the Post Master charges ten stivers for every letter received or despatched by the British Packets. The charge is under every circumstance exorbitant and falls very heavy on persons, who have extensive correspondence; hut if not warranted by law or ordinance, I consider it an extortion, which ought to he looked into hy the authorities. A moderate postage on all Island letters has on former occasions been commented on as desirable to he introduced, instead of having letters scattered about as they now are and often miscarried. The distressing cry of lire was no sooner uttered than crowds of people ushered from their lodgings ami sped with all the rapidity that life admitted, lirst to the Fire Depot where the engines were obtained and then to the conflagrated spot where they braved the ticice element and hid defiance to its progress; the women with unwearied limbs supplier! the engines with water, while me men (Porters and Mechanics principally) kept the pipes flowing and wit li indefatigable exertions and good management, with the assistance of a small Military Band were the sole means of saving a part of the town Irorn utter destruction; two rooms on the premises only were laid in ashes, 'lie dwelling and other adjoining buildings sustained but little injury. Remark on tlic treatment of Yellow Fever. (From a work on the modern practice of Physic, by Robert Thomas.) Cold water is certainly a very efficacious remedy in this fever, and when applied externally, affords very great relief to the feelings of the patient, who is frequently distressed with a sensation the burning heat ; the temperature of of skin, at ihe same time being actually raised some degrees of þÿFahrenheit s thermometer above the natural standard. It is, however, only when the heat of the body is above the natural standard, that cold water should he applied externally ; and the period of its application and the frequency of its repetition must he determined by the feelings of the patient ; for should he become chilled by it, much mischief might ensue. To avoid any fatigue to the sick, which the usual mode of applying this remedy is apt to induce, a lale writer on this fever recommends as a useful substitute, that the patient should he covered as he lies in bed with a single sheet welted with cold water, which hy evaporation will gradually reduce the temperature of his body to a proper standard. I)r. þÿM Leun has seen the lies! effects to arise from cold affusion in this fever, and tells us that, in order to heighten its power, he often premised the warm hath; and while the patient was sitting in it, he dashed two or three buckets of cold water suddenly on him, iu those e, uses where the remedy was happily aplicd, the general effc ts observed from it were, an improved recollection, great-
er cheerfulness of aspect, a diminution of heat ami anxiety, the pulse becoming

more full and equable, a tendency to sleep, and sometimes a distinct remission. Some communications of Dr. þÿO Leary, through the medium of the London Medieal Journal, further establish the good effects of the affusion of cold water in typhus icterodes. We are told hy him, that he was ordered, soon after his arrival at Barhadoes from Europe, to attend the sick of the 70th regiment at Antigua, where on his arrival, he found they amounted to about a hundred. They were chiefly affected with had the been low fever, and the mortality yelvery great; hut on his employing cold affusion judiciously, agreeably 1o Ihe rules advised hy Dr. Currie (see Typhus Milior and Gravior), very few died afterwards. lie mentions, that so sensible were the men of its efficacy being superior to any oilier remedy, and of the relief obtained from it, that in his absence they frequently entreated the officers, when duty led them to visit the hospital, to have it repeated on them. In a short history of the yellow fever which prevailed at Norfolk in America, and communicated hy l)rs. Selden and Whitehead to l)r Miller of New York, further testimony in favour of an early use of the cold affusion is produced. From the great benefit which lliese physicians experienced in their two or three first trials of it, they proceeded to recommend it afterwards with confidence. They have reported, that of all those patients to whom they had an opportunity of exhibiting this remedy on or before the second day of the attack,

In no instance did they employ the rmedy in question without the exhibition of calomel at the same time, j No disagreeable effect was produced l>y j combining the use of calomel with the j affusion of cold water; nor did the mercury occasion a salivation in a single instance, although the discharge from the bowels was scarcely as great as when it was used a'one in Ihe cure of the disease. In temperate and cold climates, where we employ affusion, it will he sufficient to take the water fresh from the spring, pump, or the sea : but in warm climates, iu order to command the full and expected effect, it will he necessary that its temperature he reduced to a low degree (as about 40 of þÿFahrenheit ther- s mometer), hy exposing it to the night air previously, or hy adding some salt to it. Much benefit will probably he derived from cold water taken internally as drink: small quantities of which, frequently repeated, have been observed to moderate the excessive heat of the body, as well as the violence of general febrile action and thirst: it is likewise efficacious in disposing the skin to perspire gently, and in preventing inflammation and irritation of the stomach. For reducing the temperature of the body to its nal it .'ill and healthy standard, and for producing a refrigerant effect in

this and other fevers of the typhoid type, we have been informed by Dr. Ciimnnng, that he has derived ihe highest benefits from either sprinkling or sponging the bodies of the sick with ardent or rectified spirits, and that lie considers ihese to he in every respect superior to cold water. To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis. Sir, Having read in the þÿ þÿAvis of the 2nd instant, an unwarrantable (to say the least of it) attack on the Gravedigger at Frederiksted, I would beg leave through the medium of your paper to say a few words on the subject. þÿ T. R. þÿE. asserts that poverty should not be a reason for denying a decent burial to the dead; I fully agree with him. But when he states, that it is the duty of the Gravedigger not only þÿ to furnish the necessary implements, but likewise to assist in the ordinary þÿmanner at the interments of paupers, it is evident that he is in the wrong. The Gravedigger is not þÿ salaried he is only paid for graves opened by him, for which purpose, he is obliged to provide himself with all the tools required and to pay his assistants. To expect, that in consequence of his being paid for the digging of graves for persons dying solvent, he should furnish the necessary apparatus gratis and assist personally at the interments of paupers, is as unreasonable as it would be in exacting, that any other individual whether in a public or private situation should labor gratis for the poor ; it would without doubt bo a very unfair manner of distributing the burthens of the i State. As it cannot, however, be denied, that the grievance complained of by þÿ T. R. þÿE. really exists, yes, I to a greater degree than stated by him, in as much as the graves of paupers very frequently are not even properly covered etc., it is certainly very desirable,

that some other measures may be adopted for the burial of the poor than the method now pursued, of having the graves of such persons dug by criminals, over whom the Gravedigger can have no control whatever. To obviate the evil, let the Gravedigger be enjoined to provide graves for poor persons, but let him be paid by the country treasury for the outlays attendant therewith, according to former usage. I am, Sir, Your obedient servant VERAX. St. Croix, 4th November 1852.

REPORT on the Compensation- Bill. (Continued from our last.) If Government had disclosed their intention, that these measures were taken in order to introduce emancipation, few planters, and only those biassed by other motives, would ever have consented. It is so far from being clear, the state of slavery could not exist any longer in the Danish West India Colonies after the emancipation in the year 1834 had taken place in the English Islands, that the contrary opinion seems to us to be the more probable one. Though, as stated above, the English emancipation took place in the year 1S34, no riotous scenes nor any signs of discontent appeared in our islands during the course of fourteen subsequent years until 1848. In several other places where negro slavery existed, no change has to this day taken place. Wo shall here as an example mention the Dutch Colonies, of which some are situated even closer to the English emancipated Colonics, than ours. These Colonies, some of which have no military force, arc notwithstanding i t ion is founded, all assertions to tlio effect that no perfectly tranquil. In the Dutch part of the island St. Martins, the Governor had, it is true, in agreement with the planters, introduced a kind i sertions had elsewhere any true basis to rest upon ; of emancipation, on account of freedom being proclaimed in the French part of the island during the French revolution in 1848. The Home Government in Holland refused, however, to sanction the act, and the negroes are there still slaves. In St. Eustatius, where there is scarcely

any military force, and in Saba, where there ave 1000 slaves and not one soldier, the same system is followed as formerly. In Curacao likewise, and even in the colony Surinam, where there arc more than 40,000 slaves, and adjacent as it is to the English possessions Demcrara and Berbicc, slavery still exists as before. Let it not, contrary to such indisputable facts, be asserted any longer, nay asserted without proof, that on account of the English emancipation, slavery could not he maintained in our Colonies. It was the measures of Government itself that slackened the tie between master and slave, that strewed the seed of discontent and impatience, that gradually undermined the system of slavery, until seditious movements arose which were not quelled. IIow then can this condition, called forth by Government, be argued as a proof for the necessity of emancipation ? If such a necessity did exist, which we cannot by any means grant, Government itself created the necessity. Regarding the imputation, that the slave owners in St. Croix at the moment desired emancipation to be proclaimed, wc must decidedly contradict it. There may have been some despondent spirits, who from fear would have sacrificed their property ; but such individual feelings can, at all events, have no weight whatever against the þÿowner right s to compensation. It was not indeed to be wondered at, if some fear did exist, since the legal force which, although reduced, was more than sufficient to quell the sedition þÿ stood neutral during

the riot. But to charge those movements to the account of the English emancipation, or to the revolution which took place in the French islands, with which St. Croix is not connected, is as void of foundation, as in reality it would have appeared unreasonable to think, that our Government should have had any serious idea and been at the point of introducing emancipation, after having seen that England had ruined her colonies by such a measure

A « ® 'M (0 A T Even the Rescript of 28th July 1847 did not give rise to any very great decrease of the value of estates, which is proved by the sale of properties during the intervening period before emancipation was proclaimed. People partly confided in the promised regulation of affairs, partly they calculated that within the expiration of twelve years many things might occur to change any present design. And lastly the owners also relied upon the justice of the King, which would not omit compensation, but suffer the decision regarding it to depend on the unfolding of circumstances, and that infallible guidance of which experience is the surest source. This was the general opinion entertained in the Colonies concerning the Rescript of 1847, which left the question of compensation completely undecided. No one doubted the justice of the King. A petition dated 21st July 1852 from some of the slave owners in St. Croix to the Diet at home for compensation, has been delivered to the Colonial Council and is subjoined as a voucher to this our report ; in this petition, and also during the discussions in our Council, mention has been made, that in the commission (appointed by another Royal Rescript dated 28th July 1847, to propose regulations in consequence of the change which was at hand), it was declared, that with respect to compensation the owner relied with full security on the þÿKing justice. s Another petition is addressed to the Colonial Council by the 3rd member for St. Thomas, con-

cerning the subject in question, which we subjoin as a second voucher to our report. It is not unlikely, as presupposed in this petition, that the Rescript about the 12 years was a principal cause of that impatience for freedom which afterwards manifested itself. But as no investigation elucidating those events has been published, other circumstances, unknown to us, may also have contributed to produce the riots that took place in St. Croix on the 2nd and 3rd July 1848, which however did not spread to the islands of St. Thomas and St. John. In these latter islands all was quiet, notwithstanding their proximity to some of the English Colonies, aud although St. Thomas has constant communication and many connections with the French islands. The þÿKing s letter patent having proclaimed that motive of generosity on which the confirmation of the Governor þÿGeneral act s of emancipalegal claim can be derived from the sanction of the State, have lost their value, even if such as-

but this is far from being the ease. The whole event was only looked upon as a demonstration, against which no opposite demonstration was made. The legal power did not even take such measures as are generally adopted in cases of popular commotions to restore peace and lawful order. How much blood it would have cost to quell this riot, none can tell ; it is however supposed, that less blood would have been sited, than was since the case ; for be it remembered, it was not until emancipation had been proclaimed, that the outrages about the country commenced. At all | events the bad impression which yielding to the demands of a riotous mob has left behind, would have been avoided ; and thus wo can in no manner I acknowledge, that the inward state of our island would, if peace and order had been restored by using the means at hand, have become worse, than in reality it has after the emancipation ! In the preamble of the draft before us it is moreover stated, that by the emancipation in the throughout English islands and the ensuing the all the slave colonies, commotions negroes were already roused to a consciousness of their natural right to liberty. To this we must observe, that if such a statement were correct, the fact would have appeared and been proved the first in those colonies, which were nearest to the English islands ; but such was not at all the case in the Dutch possessions ; and in the islands of St. Thomas and St. John, the nearest to the English islands, and having daily

communications with them, there were no commotions, no signs of discontent. It is, therefore, þÿ quite ginated improbable, that the riots the in less in the manner stated, St. Croix ori- so, when you consider the secluded situation of this island, and its spare communication with the foreign islands. We shall here remark, that the military force had by degrees been reduced to about one half of what it had been formerly, and that the militia had become incomplete and less efficient through measures taken by Government ; this being done at the very time when Government was meditating and preparing emancipation, made it likely that the impatience of the unfreo for au entire abolition of slavery was roused.

We can therefore, also from this point of view, find no grounds for refusing the slave owner a right to full compensation. we have We are of opinion, that proved fully, and as far as such things according to their naturo can be proved, that the events which happened on the other Westindia islands, did not originate the tumultuary scones at St. Croix. Wc have moreover, we think, refuted the assertion, were the slave owners by the course of events that prepared to loose their negroes without compensation. How can such an assertion be reconciled to what we have pointed out above ? How does it also correspond with the many other facts which we have not touched upon, but of which, however, for tho elucidation of the case, we shall mention a few examples : 1 . The plan designed by the Governor General and confirmed by His Majesty the King, dated the 10th April 1830, and tending to an ameliorated and more definite organisation of the free men of colour ; according to this plan no slave could be emancipated, without a sum of from Ps. 200 til 800 being deposited in the Landtreasury. 2. King Frederik the Oth, his declaration, that slave property is equally intact and inviolate with any other property. The declaration was accompanied with au order to the Governor General, to deliver up some runaway English slaves to their owners, which slaves were not even reclaimed by the English Government. Of this an advertisement was at that time inserted in the newspaper of 18th June 1833, of which we subjoin a copy

as a 3rd voucher to our report. 3. The modification made by the King in the confirmation of the Governor þÿGeneral placard s of 7th May 1838, by which modification it was declared that the payment of a monthly salary of one dollar to such slaves as were drivers or foremen on the estates, should not be considered as an obligation on the part of the slave owners. This is a clear acknowledgment on the part of the legislator, of slave service of his the þÿmasters s right to demand the without remuneration. 4. Ordinance of 1st May 1840, by which it is allowed the slaves to purchase their freedom, on appiaisement paying their value ; such þÿ in the value to be fixed by legal a manner that the master is thereby indemnified, according to the use he could have of his unfree such are the words of the law. After a declaration so clear on the part of the legislator, how could it have been believed that Government intended to abolish slavery without giving compensation to the owner ? Such a belief would be tantamount with doubting His Majesþÿty word s ! but a doubt of this nature could never gain ground among His loyal subjects in the Westindia islands. When in the remarks to the draft of law before us it is alledged as a ground for refusing compensation, þÿ that the planters instead of having a well disposed working class, both previously to the emancipation and subsequently, would in all probability, under a continued state of slavery, have had to struggle with an unwilling and hostile

slave þÿpopulation, we can not coincide in this either. As well-disposed as the working class was previously to this revolution, just as unwilling it has afterwards become. There is a general aversion to any kind of field labor, which the former unfrec by all means seek to avoid. The number of the laborers is continually decreasing, in spite of regulations to and all a the measures been introduced, put stop to this groat evil, which have which is undermining the welfare of the Colonies. Thus, according to elucidations given by the Inspector of estates in voucher Letter B, to which we beg to refer, at least 1200 individuals, belonging to the working class, and two thirds of them good laborers, had at that time left the sugar estates in St. Croix. According to the lists produced by Government, it appears that by the removals of the 1st October 1851, 267 individuals, and by removals during the year up to tho 1st October 1852, 124 individuals, have left the sugar estates in St. Croix. To this must he added, that less work is now done in a day than formerly, and that it is now more expensive than before ; in this respect we again beg leave to refer to said voucher, which throws a light also on the decrease of the value of the estates, owing to the emancipation. But even if the same power of labor was to be had, that is to say, as many estate laborers as previously to the emancipation, still the former owner has not now as before, a proportion thereof at his own disposal. When most he is in need

of it, he may not be able to get it, and realizing it in money, as he could do before, is now decidedly put out of his power. This is his direct loss ; but his indirect loss becomes still greater, if Government do not take active measures, not only to preserve the amount of labor still at hand, but also to procure necessary supplies. For otherwise the planter, besides losing his negroes, will

moreover lose his fields, works, buildings, machineries SfC. djc - 1 which in such a case would j become of no value. He would thus sustain a still greater indirect loss, than that direct loss, which he has already suffered by the emancipation of the negroes ; and his claim for compensa- j tion would thereby be greatly increased. The planters have, most assuredly, made exertions no less extraordinary than praiseworthy, in order to supply the want of labor ; new and expensive means are the used ; many have are introduced; planters steam engines applied all their strength and all their credit to contend consequence against the many difficulties that have arisen But of the alterations in question. in what thus has been done and expended, would all be lost, if a just compensation for the emancipation be not given. To be continued.

Tlic Colonial Couucil ! The first ordinary session of the Colonial Council terminated on Friday last. The question that naturally presents itself to the mind of every one on this occa- j sion, is what has been effected by the Assembly ? The answer is obvious. Nothing! Except the bill for : compensation to the the late slave owners, we are not aware, that which has been ! ! any other bill laid by duly forwarded by the House, Government before the Council has þÿprogressed not even through its first stage ! i What are we to infer from this apparent supineness on the part of Honorable Members ? Are the tasks they have undertaken superior to their capacity; or ! are the projects of laws so defective, that the respective j committees are obliged to remodel them from first to j last ? Without anticipating the reasons, which the House cannot fail soon to give the public for this procrastination, we cannot withhold the remark, that the constituencies seemingly have not much reason for being pleased with their representatives. If the delay be owing to the defectiveness of the drafts laid before the j House, it is excusable ; for many of the bills published t will no doubt work well as a whole þÿ but taken in detail will, if passed in their present state, prove failures. Such among others is the case in a very eminent degree with the bill for the regulation of trade and commerce. While we find in the bill various restrictions and taxations for the exercise of these branches of industry, we perceive no corresponding ameliorations of

the burthens under which they are now suffering, j Under such circumstances it may perhaps be better, if | these matters were postponed until the next session of the Council, at which time the Government may be j able to lay before the Assembly a detailed plan for the equalization of the various Taxes and Dues paid to the State and Communal Treasuries. With regard to the private bills, introduced during the session, we are able to say but little on the subject, as their contents have not been published. If their number could form a standard for judging their þÿ merit, we would say, they bid fairly to remedy all our griev- j þÿances. But as it would appear as that some of these measures have been characterized insignificant, until are necessitated to defer every opinion thereon, we ; they are published bv the respective movers, to who in introducing them in tile House certainly ought of have to certain promoted as no public, or all their publication, for the information the measure, whether favorable or prejudicial classes of the community, could be established as law, unless public opinion had been elicited on the matter. The sittings of the Council being now prolonged for three weeks, the public may yet expect that the business of the House will be brought to a close ere the the Council separate. But if we compare the future with the past we may find ourselves constrained not to expect much done by the Council during the extra session. For, if in four weeks only one bill has pro-

gressed through the House, ally expect dispatched in three how many can we ration- weeks ? As there are, however, some bills of paramount importance before the House, namely that of the Press and of the Budget, we would impress on the minds ot Honorable Members the necessity of passing these bills in this session. We may again return to this subject, when the private bills, referred to in the foregoing, are published. M.
