V» M þÿ PROCEEDINGS OF THE COLONIAL COUNCIL. The Eight Meeting of the Council was held on Thursday, þÿ 28thOclbr. The 1st member for Frederiksted and the 2nd member for Christiansteds District were absent on account of public business, which admitted of no delay. The Meeting was opened by a discussion of the question, bow far the form of the report of the Committee appointed on the draft of a regulation for the country schools could be considered as satisfactory or not, as it coniines itself to the proposition of sundry alterations in the draft, without having stated any motives, which according to the opinion of the Committee rendered such alterations desirable or requisite. The Chairman of the Committee, the 2nd crown member, declared, that the Speaker, the 3rd crown member, was ready by word of mouth to explain the views of the Committee that lead to its proposals and motives. The 4th member for St. Thomas district observed, that the 13th of the rules of business prescribes, that the report of a committee must be laid before the Council previous to a 1st discussion, from which rule no deviation ought to be made; to this the Speaker of the Committee replied, that be was ready to give all the elucidations that may be required, in consequence of the Commitþÿtee proposals. s The Governor observed, that the form adopted by the Committee, though unusual, was recommendable on account of its brevity. The 1st member for St. þÿJohn district s agreed with him, and proposed, that the said report should at

once be brought to the 1st reading; but that the Committee should compile written motives to the proposed alterations of the draft, before the matter was ultifor þÿFrederiksted district mately decided upon. The 2nd of member s was a contrary opinion, and demanded, supported by the 1st member for St. Thomas district, that the question should be put to the vote, whether the report should be returned to the Committee, in order that the motives might be added, before the draft was debated upon. This proposition was acceded to, and the result of the voting þÿ which was done by calling the roll þÿ was that the report þÿ with a majority of 9 against 8 votes þÿ should be returned to the Committee. The 1st member of St. Johns district, mover of No. 2 of the order of the day,

regarding the appointment of a physician in that island, explained the necessity of having a physician by royal appointment, for the benefit of a community, which was utterly destitute of all regular and satisfactory medical attendance ; the salary of said physician calculated at $1000, is the disbursement of which amount the Itoyal and Land Treasuries as well as the planters ought to contribute a part; to which the planters had previously declared themselves willing. The Governor acknowledged the great importance of the matter, and expressed his desire, that the bill be connected with the proposal regarding the reductions of the police expenditure of the said island ; the case was unanimously referred to the Budget Committee. In support of No. 3, regarding an alteration in the issuing of sea passes at St. Thomas, the mover, 6th member for St. Thomas district, with special reference to a case, which has recently occurred at St. Thomas, stated the many inconveniences connected with these passes, especially with regard to the renewal of them, and proposed that a Committee of 5 or 7 members be appointed to investigate, whether the passes in question might not be issued once for all, or that the fee derived from them be i ment to the amount of $10,001) at a imposed in some other manner ; to this the Governor remarked, that nothwithstanding he admitted, that these passes, which were already done away with in Denmark, led to many inconveniences, and besides did not afford any very great j two projects could be conjointly reali-

security, still it would not he easy to abolish them in these colonies, on account of the revenues accruing from them being tolerably considerable ; thus the whole was virtually a question of it financial nature. He added, that this matter hud already previously been brought before the Ministry, in consequence of a representation from the Royal Council of St. Thomas, recommending that nationality a tax on vessels be instituted, together wi h other alterations, which however was as yet unsettled ; he moreover declared bis willingness to receive a special bill, it being connected with the proposal of the Royal Council as within stated. The patter was unanimously referred to the Government. As regards No. 4, a bill proposing the reorganisation of the Police of $t. Thomas, the same mover, pointed out the | existing want of public safety, especially at night, as well as the general deficiencies of the whole system. He was supported by the 2nd as well as the 3rd member for St. Thomas; the latter principally dwelling upon sundry changes during latter years, in regard to the position of some public functionaries, and also the insufficient number of policemen now at the disposal of the Police administration. The mover proposed that a Committee be appointed to investigate these grievances, and to address t lie Government to that effect. The Government having already laid before the Council it proposal regarding the organisation of the Police at St. Thomas, the bill was in consequence

hereof rejected by a majority of 15 against 2 votes. With regard to No. 5, bill respecting the sum of $20,000, deposited at St. Thomas, destined for the erection of a town hospital there, the mover, 3rd member for St. Thomas district observed, that this amount was collected by an extra tax, imposed for the purpose of erecting an hospital in the town of St. Thomas, but had not as yet been appropriated as originally intended, arising from some difference in opinions between the Burgher Council and theGovernment; on the contrary the amount

On account of a previous bill brought before the Colonial Council by the last mentioned member, the Governor expressed his surprise at hearing that the þÿmover intention s was to have hospitals, the one for Mariners arid Strangers the other for the town population; lie stated, that according to preliminary estimate, the expenses attending the erection of a general hospital would amount to $23,000, whilst the sum collected for the purpose did not exceed $20,500, that Government had gratuitously given the necessary ground, and that t lie plan of the building laid before Government had been returned with divers remarks to the St. Thomas Council. The mover endeavored to prove, that the proposed hospitals for Mariners and Strangers was quite a distinct undertaking, and quite independent of an hospital for the town population, the former being solely calculated for the commerce of St. Thomas, for the erection of which the merchants only desired a loan from Govern-
moderate interest. The Governor having observed, that it would be a task devolving on the Burgher Council of St. Thomas to procure the necessary information whether the
zed, þÿ it was agreed upon, that the matter should with a strong recommendation from the Colonial Council be referred to the Government. The Chairman closed the Meeting at 2 þÿo clock.

(Q33 The following has been handed us for insertion : þÿ To the Repri sentn tires of l Vent End Jurisdiction in the Colonial Assembly. Gentlemen, The following rennrks are respectfully forward >d to you to be submitted to tile consideration of the Colonial Council, in the hope that they will give t will a patient investigation and adopt toe means of remedying the evils complained of. 1. Duties on ai tides indispensably necessary for the use of the poorer class of inhabitants should lie reduced to a low figure. A committee of business men should lie appointed to enumerate such articles, and the proper reductions made, whilst articles of luxury should have a far higher duty placed on them than is at present. 12. A protecting duly should hi placed on such manufactured articles, as are And can be in id in the island, and winch the committee above allmh d to shall also enumerate, whilst the materials for the manufacturing of them be placed under the bead of articles paying a low duty; this would then bo of benefit to tradesmen, who would thereby be enabled to sell at as low rates as the present importers. 3. With the exception of bread, candles and pork, no selling ought to lie allowed in the country, except by itinerant sellers from the towns ; the wants of the rural population can bo abundantly supplied, as formerly by such sellers, as well as by tiie opportunity afforded them on market days to lay in stores for the week. Neither should the country labourer oil non market days lie permitted to hawk about towns, fruit

and vegetables ; the practise of selling dry goods &c. in the country, by country people, injures merchants and shop keepers who pay for their license, and the practice of selling fruits &c., by them on non market days, prevents our town fruiterers or hucksters from disposing of their articles bought on market days from the country people. 4. Those who traffic in bread and cakes ought not to bo taxed, as such business can scarcely support a small family, far less admit of any additional burlm-ii 5. All masters or supercargoes of vessels without distinction, should be obliged to consign themselves to a merchant of the place, and not a- at present ho allowed to open a store, not even by paying for a iiurgliers Brief or tax ol any class. 6. Every encouragement ought to lie given the American trade on which these Islands mainly depend, and this will be effected by a speedy alteration of the tariff. The custom house charges on our island vessels, and on other vessels not Danish, call loudly for reduction, particularly the wharfage dues, a correction of which will induce the Americans to renew their trade with us. 7. Tide waiters arc chosen from among the Military who occasion much confusion by not speaking the

English language, whilst among our indigent natives can be found persons capable and willing to fill such situations. 8. The porters who are compelled to pay for a license to work as such, should be protected by a regulation to prevent transgression by ships crews, working as porters on shore in discharging or landing of cargoes, neither should sailors be hired out from their own ship to act as porters on board other vessels. The coopers and carpenters are also in like manner sufferers. 9. The Military some of whom are mechanics are allowed to perform work out of the garrison, this injures materially our mechanics who can not compete with them in low prices. 10 Sailors employed on board of the island vessels frequently leave them at the moment of sailing ; and thereby occasion a delay which is injurious to the owner, it is to be hoped that laws will be enacted to remedy this evil. 11 It is thought that the substitution of a constabulary force from among the respectable citizens would insure the public peace far better than the present system of choosing soldiers from the garrison. 1 2 Persons living on estates ought not to bo allowed to send horses to town for hire, as it deprives those in town of a livelihood who keep horses and carriage for that purpose. 13. The community would be benefitted and the þÿtraders interest best served if a law were enacted to compel the sale of certain articles by weight. 14. Those who live by tl.e rent of houses or rooms should be protected by an ap|>eal to the policemaster,

and if need be the tenant ejected by the authority of the law without cost to the landlord. At present an ejectment can only be effected by the sheriff at the enormous charge of $8 when perhaps the tenant owes but 2 dollars. The consequence is that those who cannot afford to pay the fee are compelled to house dishonest persons gratis, or forcibly drive them out and thereby incur the penalty of breaking the peace. A simple notification from the policemaster to such defaulters would Ire sullicient to cause them to vacate the premises. 15. A commission of competent persons should be appointed to regulate the amount of taxes which ought to he paid on land and buildings in town. Houses or landed property should not be sold for taxes, when the owner holds moveables of sufficient value to cover the amount in arrears, furthermore as in former times a commission should be appointed to collect taxes in this town. Hi. A common court of pleading ought to be allowed finding that in order to obtain justice in the police court the charges are much too high for the poorer inhabitants whose rights are in consequence often abused. It has been remarked that the evidence given by a |H)lic', is taken in preference ol evidence given by one or more of the inhabitants no matter how respectable tli cy may be, in consequence of this their rights are often abused. 17. In as much as the apothecary can, by paying for an additional license, sell merchandize, in the same manner merchants and store keepers should bo allowed

to sell drugs, but not compounded medicines. 18. The apothecary holding the monopoly, should b- a person competent, and of steady babits ; and the inspection to which lie is subject by the King's physician ought to be more strictly attended to, as the inhabitants are frequently imposed on by spurious medicines. 19. Fraudulent debtors should be punished with imprisonment at their own expence. 20. Necessary facilities for conducting business of every description ought to be established, before the value of burgherbrief or other licences can be known ; we therefore recommend that the regulations regarding the same, should not be enforced until further ; moreover foreigners must not on any consideration be allowed to commence business of any description without being subject to the same taxations as the inhabitants. Fredoriksted, 20th October 1852.

Likewise as it is a mistake to presume, that by the emancipation the population has been made willing to work, thus it is no less a mistake to believe, that this population would in the contrary case have become unwilling and hostile. It is a decided proof against such a mode of reasoning, that slavery, as mentioned above, still exists in many places, without even a military force to support the institution. Every one who knows the character of the slave population, must acknowledge, that they are good natured and in no wise rebellious, as long as not roused by alterations. We cannot omit on this occasion to observe, that the arguments heard in Europe about Westindian affairs are frequently entirely incorrect. It was for instance alleged at the Diet in Iloeskilde in the year 1846, as a matter of certainty, that the value of property in the colony would certainly rise considerably by the emancipation, and in consequence thereof also the mortgages belonging to the State. That the very reverse is the case, is a lamentable, but obvious fact. With these remarks on the objections, that have been brought forward, against the claim of compensation, we shall now pass to discuss the amount of compensation which is proposed. In this respect we beg leave to observe, that the average price, calculated by the normal value as published by the Governor General, according to reports from the Burgher Councils and other authorities, agreeably to the ordinance of 1st May

1840 4, was $1-32.50 pr. negro ; and it is notorious, that the current price was even much greater, and very often four times the amount of the $40 now proposed as a compensation. It is likewise notorious, that Government, in behalf of the King, had even a few years previously to emancipation sold negroes iu lots at an average price oi' $132.94, although the Stato had ahtjy then, by the measures taken, reduced the TOlue of that kind of property. From a subjoined catalogue of transfers of negro slaves or so called unfrce, that have occurred and have been recorded in St. Thomas town court within the period from 1st July 1828 to 1st July 1838, it appears, that 307 individuals were sold for $58,023, or $189 for each. And in another eataloguo, likewise subjoined, of similar transfers from 1st July 1838 to 1st July 1848, 60 individuals were sold for no more than $8617, or $143.61 for each ; showing a decrease of value to the amount of $45.39. The English Government paid an average of in said " Remarks," that in those of the £25 pr negro. To this an observation is made colonies which most fitly can be compared English to our islands, only £14 or $70 was granted in compensation pr. negro. We cannot acknowledge that our colonies are nearest in comparison to those of the English colonies, which obtained the smallest compensation But if even this comparison is justly selected, and not encroaching too much on equity, there is still a great difference between $70 cash, and $40 payable in a long space of years.

There is moreover a circumstance which has entirely been unnoticed, viz: that the act of parordered at the same time, that the compensation, slaves should be bound to the owners emancipated liament which fixed the amount of for 6 years. Another fact is likewise unnoticed, and one of still greater consequence, viz : that the English planters for many years enjoyed the whole profit of the rising sugar prices, occasioned by the decrease of the production of sugar after the emancipation ; for on foreign sugars the import duty was 64 shillings, whilst on English sugars it was only 24 shillings, thus affording a protection duty of 40 shillings or £2 (equal to $10) pr. 100 lbs. The French planters have received but little more than $90 pr. negro ; but it is expected that they will obtain a considerable addition. So much is certain, that they likewise have the of a considerable protection-duty against advantage foreign sugars. But with us the protection duty is but 92 Rigsbankskillings or about 50 cents The proposed 40 dollars cannot thus pr. in any way 100 lbs. be esteemed as even an approximate of the amount which indisputably the former slave compensation ownors have a right to, a compensation which Government itself acknowledges to be founded on justice and equity.

It is a maxim in the law of the country, that no one can be deprived of his property, unless the common weal demands it, and then oniy with full compensation. This was proclaimed by the Placard of 31st July 1841, and this right has become still more sacred and inviolable by the fundamental law 87, to which we appeal, contending that Government cannot, without breaking this law, refuse to give full compensation, at all events such a compensation as will correspond to that which other States have not refused their subjects. The average value of the slaves, according to the statement made by the Inspector of the King's estates (voucher b. page 36) must be between 128 and 16J dollars. Of theso amounts the average is 144 dollars, inakiug with the interest from 3d July 1848 until 31st December 1852 at 6 pr. ct. $182.88. The demand of interest from 3d July 1848 is in every respect perfectly entitled, being implied by the natural as well as by the legal sense of compensation. The ministry has observed, that the colonies can not decline defraying a proportionate share of the losses and burdens which have devolved on the mother country during the latter years. The

Colonial Council admit this demand as lair on the part ot the mother country ; and, calling to wind that the voluntary and not inconsiderable contributions towards public expenditure, which were remitted from here during the war, bear testimony of the readiness with which the inhabitants of these islands are animated, even during hardships oi their own, to assist the mother country in her hour of need, we make no objection that a proportionate bhare of the expenses incurred by the losses and burdens of the war, which might be calculated aecoiding to the number of inhabitants, be deducted from the full amouut of compensation which we consider a legal claim on the part of the colonies. We likewise admit it to be a just demand, that the col mies themselves should sustain a proportionate share ol the loss incurred by the emancipation. We furthermore take iuto consideration, that to be the right which hae boon abolished, and which is compensated, was generally looked upon with repugnance, and that the continuance of the slave institution distanced the colonies from that good feeling and sympathy in the mother country, which it is to be hoped will now, bince the abolition ol the institution, no longer be withheld. All circumstances duly regarded, it is the opinion of the Colonial Council that an average piiee ot not less than $75 lor each unfrcc, emancipated on the 3d of July 184o, will be accepted m these islands as a somewhat satislactory compensation. Conscious that, on the part of the inhabitants

of these islands, all will be done to contribute readily, and as far as they are able, towaids the end of being united more strongly with the mother country, the Colonial Council rest in confidence that the mother country, on her part, will not deem the burden heavy, to let justice be done to the colonies. In consequence of the claim of compensation being, in the opinion of the Colonial Council, a legal one, we think that the limitation of the right ol mortgageholders, as proposed in the 6 ol the draft ol the Ministry, ought to bo omitted. and no boilers to make steam, and no place to put them if they were wanted. No smoke, and no chimneys worth naming. No more hiss and roar, no more explosion. Hereafter all is to be dry and still. This is the caloric ship. A costly experiment truly, and, if successful, destined to work an entire revolution in mechanics, nothing less than an entire disuse of steam as a motor. There is something sublime in the daring displayed in this undertaking ; a single invention entering the lists and challenging the perfected work of ages. The daring wins attention and commands intensest interest. The marine steam-engine is the result of years of experiment and study, and consequent progress. A very few years ago no workshop in the world would have dared to undertake such massive work. Castings of 40 tons wt., and complicated to the last degree; shafts of wrought iron welded up big as a pine tree; cylinders large enough for a coin fortahle bedroom. Had any man dared devise the work and execute the drawings, no shop could have satisfied the conditions; hut now, by short, and slow, and easy steps, every dimension has been increased inch by inch, until at last our engines seem like the very wheels and machinery of nature. We build iron caverns, pour in an ocean, and set them over volcanoes, and modestly call them boilers and furnaces, as it were a mere device to boil eggs withal. A pair of first-class side-lever marine engines, slowly swinging their immense proportions to and fro in ponderous silence, ap-

proach as near to sublimity as it is lawful for the work of man to come. He that can look upon them with no emotion of awe, and no thrill of apprehension, will do well to be anxious at once about bis soul. Notwithstanding this, and unabashed by the imperial renown and majesty of the modern engine, there is come an unknown champion into the lists to dispute the empire and claim the first rank to itself. Not by slow steps of progress does it propose to rise to dominion. Not by a long apprenticeship or slavery to pumps, mills, ferries, and river boats, the steps by which steam attained to Royalty, þÿ not so will the caloric engine win its way. All or nothing. All at once, or nothing. And so the hull is builded and launched, such a hull as has never before been set afloat for beauty, strength, and costliness. Her register is over 2,000 tons. There are not ten steamers in the world larger than she, and not one of equal workmanship in respect of seaworthiness and strength. Her engines are built with the same elegance and precision that we should anticipate they were the .'30th instead of the first of their kind. Four huge cylim.ers, each 13 feet in diameter 00 inches is þÿ the largest diameter the writer ever saw given to a steam cylinder þÿ are to be set in a line along the keel. Under each is a little furnace, having two small firedoors, each furnace capable of holding, perhaps, three or four bushels of coal. A ton of anthracite will start them all. Each pair of cylinders constitute an en-

gine. Their united power is transmitted to a single crank upon the main shaft. The agent that is to give motion is air, expanded by the beat of the furnaces already named. The detail of valves, Ac., must be, in effect, identical in all reciprocating cylinder engines, whatever be the motor. In the caloric engine the valve chests are just like those in use in the ordinary 1 þÿbeam-engine. In a word, the caloric engine is a steam-engine made to go by elastic expansive air at a low pressure, instead of elastic expansive steam at a higher pressure. Hence the necessity of so many and so enormous cylinders ; for, the pressure upon each square inch of piston-head being less

& <Q 'Jt <B '1 A T !X 3 than in a steam engine, of course the area, or number of square inches, must be increased by the same ratio or factor that measures the decrease of pressure if we would secure equivalent effects in the two cases. This is done by fourfolding the area of each cylinder, and by doubling their number. Four 13-feet cylinders, with a pressure of I lb. to the inch, friction aside, will yield as much power as one cylinder 78 inches in diameter, with 1(5 lbs. pressure to the square inch. The advantages claimed for the caloric engine are imposing. I. Economy of space. A þÿmoment inspection s justifies and admits this claim. 2. Safety from explosion and accident. This, too, is undeniable. 3. Incidental ventilation for the entire ship, since it is proposed to draw the supplies of air from the þÿship h s ull. This, also, seems indisputable. 4. Economy in first cost. The engine is about equal in cost to a steamengine, and hence saves the cost of boilers, having no use for them. «3. Economy in running, requiring but one-tilth the men. writer cannot hazard an opinion, not having seen the soul of the invention, þÿ the þÿregenerator, as the inventor has christened it, an attachment sustaining the same relation to a caloric engine that a þÿ condenser does to a steam engine. There is no question as to whether air will expand by heat ; expanding, it will drive a piston, no doubt; about these elemental postulates there can be no question. Midst air will expand by higher ratios than dry air; hut even dry air will increase its volume over -10 per cent ; by receiving 93 degrees of lie it : ordinary atmospheric air increases its volume 50 percent, bet ween zero and the

Hut the question, þÿ can air lie quickly heated and quickly cooled ; can it be made to shrink in the cylinder instantly, as steam does when it escapes into the condenser ? þÿ which the writer cannot ahswer. Captain þÿEricsson þÿ s regenerator is intended to accomplish this. It is to heat the air as it rushes into the cylinder, and cool Hie air, or receive hack the heat, all but 34 or 43 degrees lost by radiation, as the air makes its escape. Furthermore, it is to discharge this office promptly, instantly, so that the slend rest volume will, on entering, become round, and stout, and portly as an alderman ; but, on retiring, unlike the alderman, will disgorge its gettings, and go forth slim as it came, and leave its beat and sudden portliness for the next occupant. The furnaces have need to supply only the little loss of 3) degrees or so out of 430 or 590 which the air receives by inheritance from its predecessors, merely the leakage by munition. Such claims as these excite scepticism. They do not necessarily involve an absurdity, and if the þÿ regenerator will do what is claimed to be doing already in an experimental engine, then beyond a question the caloric engine will worn, and the days of steam are numbered. A few weeks will settle the question. The Ericsson is afloat, and her engines are well nigh complete. Expectation is on the þÿtiptoe. to reveal himself to the world by deeds, not words, the whole nation would have been by this time on the tiptoe of expectation with regard to the experiment in preparation under his superintendence.

If' the caloric engine shall prove to be all that is predicted for it, Captain Ericsson has made a discovery more important than any one which has startled the world since the invention of the locomotive We will just set down the claimed advantages of the caloric over the steam engine, and every reader will perceive the sweepings and stupendous nature of the revolution in all material affairs which its success will gradually effect ; I, The caloric engine burns about onetenth as much fuel as a steam-engine; hence a caloric ship of the largest size may circumnavigate the globe without stopping to take in coal ; hence not a sail will ever be seen on the ocean in 50 years after the success of the new principle is certain; hence, machinery will be applied to a thousand arts which now require manual labour ; hence, the possibility of the machine-plough ; and hence the coming of that good time when arduous manual toil will absolutely cease under the sun. 2. The cost of tfie caloric engine is about the same as the steam-engine, minus the cost of the boilers. 3. Only one-fourth as many engine-men will be required on board a caloric ship as are necessary for a steamer. 4. No smoke whati ver will issue from a caloric furnace when anthracite is used, and consequently no huge, unsightly smokethey work? A tough question. The j pipe will be necessary, and the rigging will be as clean as that of a sailingship. 5. There can be no bursting or collapsing of boilers, for the simple rea-

son that there will be no boilers to burst. The worst accident that can happen to a caloric engine is for it to stop ; nor is watchfulness imperatively required, as in no case can a dangerous accident occur G. Owing to the extreme simplicity of the caloric engine, the wear and tear will lie very slight, and the duration of the engine proportionally long. And the reader must bear in mind that these are not merely the confident anticipations of an ardent inventor. Two engines on the caloric principle already boiling point. (Enrt/c. That ship, which has been worthily named the þÿEricsson, will be launch) d in a day or two, and is expected to make her trial trip about the 1st »f November. If the Ericsson proves a success, that trip will justly he regarded as i lie great event of the year 1852. We have called the caloric a new principle, but it is not. The Ericsson will lie propelled by the same force as that which causes the draught in a warm room, a hurricane in the tropics, a breeze on a

þÿsummer dav, s a north-wester in winter, and every other movement of the air, namely, the expansion of atmospheric air by heat. Captain þÿEricsson scaloric engine will have inside of it a caged hurricane, artificially produced, and perfectly under command. The expanded uir will work the piston just as steam does, with the following most important difference When a portion of steam has done its work in imparting to the piston ono movement, that portion escapes and cools, that is, ceases to ho steam, and new steam Ims to lie created to supply its place; hence the vast consumption of fuel. But in the caloric engine it is otherwise. The hot air, after having given a stroke to the piston, does not escape, but it is caught and raged acain yielding back to the reservoir all but about 30 degrees ol its heat out of the 480 which it had when il entered the cylinder; hence the economy of the caloric engine. REPORT To Ilis Majesty. The 1st member for the electoral district of St. John, has moved in the Colonial Council for the emanation of a ROY AL ORDINANCE, by which a duty to the Land Treasury of St. John he imposed on HORSES and BOATS in the island, according to the tenor of the subjoined draft. During the debates on this motion, tli e same has been supported on the following grounds : That the Land Treasury of St. John, being, since tho emancipation in 1848, almost entirely without revenues, and loaded with a continual increase of debt I as well to the State Treasury as to private persons, cannot, without injury thereby being caused, remain in this condition until the time may come, when a reform of the taxation of the Colonies, as intended by Government, will be undertaken; furthermore: That the duties in question þÿ which have originally been proposed by a Commission, consisting ot the judge and the members of the Burgher Council and appointed in order to take into consideration, and make proposals tor regulating the future taxation of the island þÿ are requisite for defraying the most urgent expenses of the municipality, for covering which no other means are known to lie at hand, say in particular the expenses for maintenance of prisoners and for tile conveyance ot the post, also such uncertain expenses as in cases ot' accident may he required for persons in distress, regarding which different expenses the amount ot the duties, being calculated at about
8189 annually, might in some degree he sufficient for the present; finally: That

the duties proposed are moderate, and that in part, or rather principally they would fall upon persons who now contribute nothing towards the public expenditure of the island. On the other hand it has been urged during the discussions: That, whereas it is the emancipation which has deprived the Land Treasury of its principal revenue, the capitation-tax, and whereas the duties now proposed in a great measure would fall upon persons who by the emancipation likewise have sustained a greater or smaller, but at all events the parties concerned very considerable loss of property, it would not be consistent with equity, if such sufferers should contribute by the imposition of new taxes to compensate the loss of the Land Treasury, while their own just claim for compensation remains unpaid ; the less so, because the loss which these parties have sustained by the emancipation is so hardfelt, that it lias made it extremely difficult to them to defray the burdens that already are incumbent on them, and in some cases has even caused owners to abandon their properties and quit the island; it has also been called into memory, as for the estate-owners, that the export-and custom-duties which they have to pay amount to upwards of 11 per cent of the gross produce of sugar and rum, and sometimes, by means

calculated, still more. For these last mentioned reasons the Colonial Council with 10 votes against 7 has thought proper, not at present to recommend the adoption of the proposal ; whereas the Council, at the same time, with 15 votes against 1 has agreed to recommend the economical situation of the Land Treasury of St. John to the particular rare ot'yonr Majesty's Government. Thus the present most submissive report is rendered.

REPORT To His Majesty. The Colonial Council having been charged by the Government to make REPORT relative to the proposed extension to these islands of the LAW of 3rd January 1851 regarding tITe use of the "PRESS" do hereby declare that we agree in opinion, that the said law ought to lie extended to the Colonies, in consideration of, that the lately established deliberative representative Body cannot forbear that general developemcnt of ideas, which can only he obtained by the means of a Free Press. We also declare ourselves in favor of the supplement to said law, proposed by the Government, viz: the necessary prefatory regulation, that every individual shall he at liberty to publish his opinion, and that the censureship he done away with ; þÿ all with due regard to the existing rules ordained by law. A majority of 15 votes against 1 has deemed it advisable, that a penalty he prescribed for offences against foreign Colonial Governments, and propose therefore as letter b (in consequence whereof letter b and c in the 2nd draft will become letter c and d): " The punishment of fines as per paragraph 7 and from the supposition entertained in the conclusion of the same, shall be applicable in cases of the therein mentioned offences directed against foreign Colonial Governments." A minority has been of opinion, that sub letter a, in the draft, after the words: class" be inserted : " or instigates or "contemptuous language toward any incites to resistance against the State or
the Government ;" this opinion is based upon, that not every practicable or physical resistance can he treated according to the 5th paragraph of the law, the pro-

vision of which docs not give that guarantee which might he required in these colonies. A minority has also thought proper to recommend, that there he added to contents : " should any of those offences the draft a regulation of the following treated of in the 9th paragraph he directed against the Governor, such shall be subject to public prosecution." These proposals were however rejected by the Council, the former by 10 votes against 6, þÿ the latter by 14 votes against 2. Finally the Colonial Council do unanimously and most submissively propose that the draft with the amendments agreed upon be made into law.
